maintopic: INITIAL PRICES FOR WESTERN WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: INITIAL PRICES FOR WESTERN WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY
speechtext:
I would like to advise the house of the decision of the government in regard to initial prices for western wheat, oats and barley for the crop year commencing August 1, 1952.
As members of the house know, the Canadian wheat board is in the midst of a very large and difficult operation this year. In spite of unfavourable harvesting conditions last fall, and in spite of the fact that there is considerable threshing to be completed in the prairie provinces, the outturn from 1951 grain crops in the west is still very large.

Grain
It is likely that total grain deliveries by western producers in the present crop year will be in the neighbourhood of 700 million bushels, which is the largest delivery of grain in any single crop year in the history of the west.
The difficulties of the present crop year have not arisen from the quantity of grain which will be delivered to the board. The difficulties arise from the lateness of the 1951 harvest, the unprecedented quantity of out-of-condition grain threshed by producers, and the general quality of the grain harvested. In spite of these difficulties, good progress has been made in disposing of deliveries from the 1951 crop. The large crop in 1951 was accompanied by a good demand for grain, and this fact will be reflected in the operating results attained by the board during the crop year, in spite of all the difficulties arising from the lateness of the crop, delayed harvesting, and the fact that at least 250 million bushels of grain will be received from producers in a tough or damp condition.
So far as wheat is concerned, the major part of producers' deliveries during the crop year 1951-52 will be disposed of within the crop year. However, with the prospect of substantial marketings by producers in the final months of the crop year, some increase in the wheat carry-over can be expected' on July 31 next.
On the basis of progress to date in disposing of the 1951 wheat crop, and the prospect for a continuation of a broad demand for wheat, the government is establishing the initial price for wheat for 1952-53 at the same level as at the start of the present crop year, namely, $1.40 per bushel basis No. 1 northern wheat in store at Fort William-Port Arthur or Vancouver.
In general, the position in respect to oats and barley parallels that of wheat. While very large deliveries of both grains are expected during the present crop year, demand has been satisfactory. There will be some increase in year-end stocks of both grains, due to the lateness of the 1951 harvest, the volume of grain still to be threshed this spring and the necessity of conditioning large quantities of oats and barley prior to sale. However, the outlook is such that the government feels justified in establishing initial prices for both oats and barley at the same level as at the start of the present crop year. These initial prices are 65 cents per bushel basis No. 2 C. W. oats in store Fort William-Port Arthur, and 96 cents per bushel basis No. 3 C. W. 6-row barley in store Fort William-Port Arthur.
As I have mentioned on other occasions, these are initial prices, and it is always the

hope of the government that pooling operations conducted by the wheat board will result in surpluses which will permit either increases in the initial prices during the crop year, or final payments to producers after the close of the crop year, or both.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned on Friday last I had just read the motion moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on Monday, October 22, 1951. This is one of the most important motions that has ever been passed by the house in peacetime, and for the sake of continuity I am going to read it again. It is as follows:
That this house approves the continuation of Canada's participation in the efforts being made through the United Nations to establish international peace, and in particular to defeat aggression and restore peace in Korea, and by the North Atlantic treaty nations to deter aggression and promote stability and well-being in the north Atlantic area.
I do not say that in assenting to this motion opposition members agreed with everything that the government or the services had done in connection with Korea and the North Atlantic treaty. I do say, however, that there was a wide opportunity, indeed an invitation, for anyone who did not agree 55704-78
National Defence
with everything that had been done, to say so. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) did not say so. He said so just six months later, long after the brigade had arrived in Europe as announced, arranged and carried out. The military expert of the opposition said nothing about armour.
You know, Mr. Speaker, it is sometimes not a bad thing to go back and look at what has been said previously, in order to get our perspective right. When we were raising the 25th brigade to go to Korea we did not get much in the way of support or assistance from the Conservative opposition. This is what the hon. member for Nanaimo said in the house about the 25th brigade on September 1, 1950, at page 131 of Hansard:
The appeal was made to the young men of Canada. That appeal has been magnificently responded to. But what have we got? A conglomeration of men bearing the proud names of great units, unknown to their own special unit commanders, their officers, their N.C.O.'s. Any man who has had any experience in the service will tell you that it takes a long time to weld such groups of men together in order that they become a fighting team, because it is team work that counts, not merely the individual skill of an individual soldier to handle his weapon.
Then on page 133 the hon. member also said:
I fear that the brigade now in training will be ready either too late or just in time to take part in the victory parade.
That is the brigade which everyone who has seen it says is the finest fighting formation ever fielded by this country. So much has been said about this excellent brigade that there is no need of repeating it here. We are proud of them, and they are perpetuating the famous records of Canadian soldiers who have preceded them in other wars. I wonder what they think now of the remarks made about them by the hon. member for Nanaimo.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) was not doing a service to the reserve forces when, by inference, he tagged them as he did. One or two isolated cases of personnel joining up only to participate in athletics does not mean that other units allow this sort of thing. I hope he has done as he suggested he would-that is, given the information to the minister. I do not mean that when conditions exist which are contrary to the rules and regulations and/or not in the public interest, they should not be exposed. Far from it; I am sure every citizen has an obligation in this regard, and especially members of parliament. When any of these cases come to light hon. members should report them immediately to the

National Defence
authorities or to the minister, instead of waiting for an opportune time to arrive to air the matter on the floor of the house.
It was reported immediately.

That is not what you said in the house. Adverse publicity such as this is detrimental to recruiting for the reserve army and tends to lower the morale of those at present on strength.
We are also proud of the 27th brigade; and speaking of this brigade Waldo Frank in the Los Angeles Times, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of February 6, 1952, stated it was-
-the most cheering sight in the otherwise drab picture of western defence along the Ehine-Alps line.
Further in the same article he said:
. . . although the Canadians have been in Germany only since December, they already present a better picture of a battle-ready fighting team than any other allied combat unit in Europe with two exceptions-the U.S. 1st infantry division and the two brigades of the U.S. armoured cavalry.
A little further on he says:
Everybody in the brigade is a volunteer, with full understanding of why he is here and how long he will stay in Germany. Finally, all hands in the brigade are well clothed, well fed and well paid.
Canada has only fourteen million people, but the opposition experts talk as if we should supply the military components which would normally be supplied by a country with ten to fifteen times our population. We must continue to play our part in preserving peace, and there must be visible proof of our intentions. The peoples of Europe have been liberated once and they are not interested in having it done again. We must stop communist aggression where it is. Canada has provided the troops as agreed under NATO. They asked for and got infantry. Being a member of the armoured corps I am not talking against armour. I am simply insisting that armour must be properly supplied and used. Otherwise the results are disastrous.
All the opposition theories in favour of an armoured brigade group being sent to Germany instead of the infantry brigade group we did send are another example of the opposition's apparent non-constructive attitude toward most government legislation and policies.

Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to debate Canada's national defence policy as it now exists and as it is forecast for 1952-1953, because it is difficult to grasp anything clearly from the statement made by the minister in introducing this debate on Thursday of last week. I do not mean it was difficult to understand what the

minister said; he did give us some background in connection with defence, but it was extremely difficult to get from his statement any clear picture of the present position of our defence forces, exactly what we have in the way of forces in being today to meet aggression, and what exactly we may have in the way of forces in being at the end of this fiscal year as a result of the money we are being asked to spend.
I can only say that in reading over the speech carefully with a view to getting something from it which one might criticize sensibly and constructively, there seemed to be in it a complete sense of unreality. You cannot take that speech and analyse it, and say that for this expenditure of $2,100 million we are getting so many tanks, we are going to have so many guns, we shall have so many operational squadrons at the end of the year equipped with so many aircraft of such and such a type. That sort of break-down is impossible, however carefully you examine the minister's statement. It is impossible to take from his remarks anything more than a general statement of objectives for the end of 1954.
It is true the speech was lengthy. That was quite proper, because he was introducing an important subject, having to do with an expenditure of over $2 billion. The minister did give us the background of some of the decisions that have been taken as to the raising of our forces and the objective proposed for the end of the three-year program on which we have now embarked. He gave us some lengthy quotations from the statement by General Eisenhower, which already had received ample publicity in the press and over the radio. He then gave us a definition of "infrastructure", and referred to the word as having been drawn from a French word having to do with railways.
He went on to tell us that the word was first used in the western union countries, and he referred to all the uncertainty that surrounded it, until I began to wonder whether he was going to end up by suggesting that this subject be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines rather than the committee on defence. For all we got out of the minister's speech in the way of facts upon which we might build a constructive debate, he might almost as well have been speaking about something to do with railways, canals and telegraph lines. When he referred to the western union, the threatened strike in the Western Union Company in the United States made me wonder whether we were not going to bog down to an equal extent in the creation of a defence effort in Canada.

The lack of reality in the minister's approach to this subject, and his reluctance to give us a clear statement of what we are to get for the money we are spending, is I believe typical of the situation we find when we look into the actual structure of our defence program. I can find it nowhere better illustrated than by an experience I had last year during a long week end-while the house was adjourned, not one of the Thursday to Tuesday variety-while driving back to Ottawa from Windsor. En route I gave a lift to a soldier who was wearing the shoulder flashes of the Royal Canadian Regiment. I asked him whether he had yet been with his battalion, and he told me he had been posted to the battalion shortly after joining up and had then been sent to an army cooking school. I thought that was interesting, because here was a soldier who was a member of a parachute battalion, one of the units of the airborne brigade, and I wondered what kind of cooking equipment they used. I asked him what kind of stoves they used, and said I wondered whether they were anything like the company cookers which we used in the field in the last war.	[DOT]
The soldier asked me what kind of outfit we had used, and I described to him as best I could what we called the hay-burner with the series of stands on which the containers were placed in which the food was cooked for the company. I said I did not believe that would be a suitable thing for packing and dropping from a parachute, and he said, "No, we do not have anything like that; we were not trained on that." I thought they were probably trained on something much more up to date and realistic, so I asked what kind of equipment they were trained to use. He said, "We have the most wonderful up to date sitoves in the world, a most magnificent set of gleaming Moffat electric ranges." I thought that was typical-to train a cook who is going to cook for a parachute regiment on a Moffat electric range. I did not like to ask the soldier, but I think I should like to hear from the minister what arrangements are being made for the soldier-cook to plug his stove in when he drops by parachute from an aircraft. Well, of course the illustration can be strained, but it indicates the sense of unreality pervading the whole defence structure in which we are trying to carry on this debate today.
The task is made much more difficult by the fact that the minister sought in advance, during the course of his introductory speech, to frighten us from criticizing the way in which his department is carrying out its responsibilities. When we turn to the subject of equipment, what do we find? There have been so many boasts about the money we are spending- boasts completely unmatched by equal figures of what we are getting-that it is definitely disturbing to see how little we have actually secured to date in the way of equipment. In this matter I believe the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) has to take an equal share of responsibility with the Minister of National Defence. It must be admitted that in this regard we have been, to some extent, bedevilled by difficulties over the question of standardization; but I believe that our difficulties-big enough as they were in that field-were increased by a mistaken and too early decision to standardize on American patterns. The decision to standardize on American patterns-and we must be clear on this matter-did not refer only to certain specific and individual types which we felt, in the individual case, were the most desirable on which we could standardize. The decision went much further than that. It went most of the way, if not all the way, to a decision to standardize the equipment of whole divisions on the American pattern. As authority for that conclusion I refer to the statements of the Minister of Defence Production himself, in his report to the house given in February of last year, commencing at page 179 of Hansard, and the white paper on defence to which I have already made reference and in which you find such passages as this one on page 26, where, referring to the shipment to Europe of the arms for a complete division, it says:
This procedure was the only practical way for Canada to standardize on U.S. patterns.
Throughout the white paper and throughout the speeches of the Minister of Defence Production and of the Minister of National Defence over the past year, up until the present time, there have been repeated references to this decision to standardize on the American pattern. One result of this decision-which, as I have said, was an early and mistaken one-is -that we in Canada completely lack any adequate armoured formation. Recently we have received, I understand, a few tanks of the British Centurion type for training purposes. We are not in any position-and we are not beginning to approach the position-where we could equip and field an armoured regiment, let alone a brigade with tanks.

I believe that this lack of armaments is one of the most serious criticisms of the defence preparedness of the Canadian army today. It is now apparent that not only members of the opposition but sometimes even members of the government and ministers of the crown are wiser in their hindsight than they were in their foresight. We are now told that the Centurion tank has been recognized and approved as the most suitable tank in existence, in production at the present time, for modern warfare. The Minister of Defence Production has always resolutely set his face against the proposal that Canada build tanks. It is difficult to compete with the minister in a field of this type. He makes these statements-and they are accepted as gospel- that it is not logical for Canada to build operational combat tanks. But I cannot see why-

Another example of serious deficiency in equipment, in spite of the expenditure of nearly five billions of dollars which we will have made by the end of this fiscal year, is in the lack of an up-to-date aircraft carrier. It was suggested, not just recently but some time ago, that the carrier was then obsolescent, and it is suggested that it is now obsolete. One cannot talk carelessly about replacing an aircraft carrier as though it were something that could be done overnight or even in a year. But we have not been told of any steps being taken to replace [DOT]-not just to overhaul-the Magnificent, and to have an aircraft carrier capable of handling jet aircraft, which surely must be the minimum if we are to assume the antisubmarine role which has been assigned to us.
I turn now to the question of our reserve force. It is most regrettable that there was nowhere in the minister's statement any mention worthy of the name of Canada's reserve forces. Perhaps that is not as strange as it might seem at first sight, because it is my belief, after consultation with officers in the reserve army, and after reading some of the statements made by the defence association, that so far as the preparedness of our reserve force is concerned, so far as their readiness for mobilization is concerned, it is a matter of shame and regret and not one of pride. I use those words deliberately, and I want to make it clear that it is not the fault of the officers and men of the reserve forces, but rather the fault of the system under which they are compelled to work.
This deficiency with respect to our reserve force carries more significance and more cause for alarm and disturbance when we read the minister's statement made in the house on February 5 of last year when he was referring to the general subject of defence. Speaking in the' house on that occasion the minister, describing Canada's role and obligation to contribute forces to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, said, as reported at page 95 of Hansard:
In addition to whatever army forces we have in Europe-
And that is of course the 27th brigade now over there.
-our army role in NATO is to provide a strategic reserve.
As has been pointed out, a strategic reserve in that sense does not mean anything like the reserve forces we have in Canada. A strategic reserve must be a reserve available to be placed in the field immediately as and when strategic reserves are needed- not a reserve which can be called up by a leisurely process of mobilization such as we knew in Canada when, at the time of the last
IMr. Fulton.]
war-and we were working under the same system then-it took us four years to mobilize five divisions. It is not that type of reserve at all, not a lengthy and leisurely mobilization of non-permanent forces until they are ready for the field. This type of strategic reserve refers to quite another concept of reserve forces.
Not only is the department to be criticized because we are not remotely prepared to discharge that type of obligation, in view of the sad state of Canada's reserve force, but it is imperative that we be informed by the minister what has happened to change the picture to such an extent that we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) declaring recently in the house that Canada has no commitments to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization beyond the one brigade now in Europe, and that that is the limit of our commitments up to 1954. That was the very clear statement made in the house a couple of weeks ago by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I should like to know how that statement is to be understood when it is read in conjunction with the earlier policy statement of the Minister of National Defence, that one of Canada's roles in NATO is to provide a strategic reserve.
In dealing with this subject of our reserve force, mention must be made of the Canadian rangers. When one talks to men out in British Columbia who had experience with the Pacific coast militia rangers during the last war, one realizes that there is obviously a tragic waste of the services of these men who are able and willing to make a most valuable contribution to the defence effort of this country. I should like to put in a word with the minister for the organization of the Canadian rangers, if that is what they are to be called-instead of the Pacific coast militia rangers-that at least in British Columbia he should let them be organized on a basis which has some semblance of reality. There are men out there who know how this should and could be done. Yet, so far as I am able to learn, their advice has been completely disregarded, with the result that the organizational structure of the Canadian rangers in British Columbia is completely unworkable.
What has happened? Apparently someone sat down in Ottawa and drew a series of lines on the map, dividing the province into zones and allocating one unit to a zone. In some cases these zone boundaries follow the lines of rivers. The result is that communities which have a complete identity of interest with other communities in the area find themselves on the other side of the line on the map, and thus in another zone, and

not placed with a community just across the river, or perhaps up the stream a little way on the other side of the river-they find that they are not placed with communities with which they have constantly and normally worked in matters of this kind.
This is just one further example of the state of unreality in our defence planning. It would seem that someone sits down and draws a line on a map, without consulting anyone who has had experience as to what would be the best way of organizing the Canadian rangers in British Columbia, either with reference to the proper boundaries of a zone, or the size and type of unit to be organized in a zone.
All this adds up to a situation which is desperate-and this applies to all aspects of defence preparedness, navy, army and air force, the state of equipment and the state of reserves, with which I include the Canadian rangers, formerly known as the Pacific coast militia rangers in British Columbia-all this indicates a situation that is desperate when viewed in terms of the money we have spent already and the money we are being asked to authorize this year.
Although we will have spent just under $5,000 million on defence by the end of this fiscal year, a careful review of what we have been told, read in the light of what we have not been told but should have been told, produces the numbing realization that those who are planning our defence and its integration with our North Atlantic allies are moving in a sphere as far removed from reality as it is possible to be.
What do we have? We have a navy stated to be primarily a submarine hunting force but with only one obsolescent carrier and so far as can be ascertained no additional or new carriers called for. Let me just refer to what the white paper on defence said with regard to the navy, as is found on page 7 of that document, as follows:
It has been demonstrated in the past that carriers and their aircraft are essential to the successful execution of naval action; especially is this so in the case of anti-submarine warfare which is expected to be a vital commitment of the Royal Canadian Navy in the event of another war.
We have a navy with only one obsolescent carrier and no plans made for additional or new carriers.
We have an army of three isolated and independent brigades, not trained to operate together and totally without armour. The brigade in Europe is virtually an orphan. There is no complete picture as to what operational role that brigade will be called upon to fill, under whose command it will be and with what formation it will serve. We
National Defence
have an army of 49,000 men without even a formation of division size, completely without reserves and with no reserve unit capable of immediate mobilization. We have an army where it is typical for cooks for a parachute battalion to be trained on electric ranges.
We have an air force with a conglomeration of aircraft, some jet-powered and some piston-engined. Many of the jets are obsolete; the piston-engine class are even more so. The special Canuck interceptor fighter is not even commencing production after we have spent scores of millions of dollars and after many loud boasts have been made about the imminence of the production of these aircraft in numbers.
We have an army which is virtually at a standstill with respect to equipping and training on new and up-to-date materials, with all the difficulties and delays that are imposed on training because of the premature and unwise decision to standardize on United States lines. That has apparently been now abandoned except with respect to some artillery weapons. This is not being wise after the event because we warned the minister of the dangers of an early decision to standardize on United States lines. We told him that in our opinion that decision should not be taken. It would be interesting to know, and I think we must be told, how much time and money has been wasted as a result of this decision and what the backing away from it will make necessary in the way of additional expenditure.
We find a situation where at the time of the last white paper 56,000 civilian personnel on a full and part-time basis were required to look after a defence force of 80,068, or nearly two civilians for every three service personnel. The proportion today is as great or even greater according to the information the minister has given.
This is a situation which is bristling with questions requiring answers, not evasions; requiring answers as to what is being done to bring our reserves into a state of readiness; whether mobilization will be made possible in a reasonable time and not a matter of years. It requires answers as to what is being done to make Canada well equipped with fighting tanks. What is being done as to standardization? What is being done so as to equip our air force with adequate armament? What is being done to equip and prepare our navy to discharge its submarine hunting role which has been laid down so clearly for it?
It is a situation that indicates without room for argument that the minister has a heavy responsibility to answer for a story of errors, inadequacies, waste, duplication and inefficiency.

National Defence
In closing I want to contrast this situation with some of the words which the minister used toward the end of his statement when he told us that to criticize would be only to say, "yes, but," and that to criticize would somehow or other be merely a display of hindsight. We are being asked to authorize the spending this year of $2,100 million. That being so, is anyone more entitled to say "yes, but" than the taxpayer, when he is the man who must pay the taxes from which this money is to come?
Surely the taxpayer is entitled to ask this question-or to have his elected representatives in parliament ask it for him. Does the minister really mean to say, when fifty cents out of every tax dollar asked for in this year's estimates is going to be spent by his department, that the taxpayer has no right to say, "yes, but"? Does he mean to say that the taxpayer has no right to say: Yes, I am willing to put up the fifty cents, but I think it would be better spent if it was spent on giving us a little more up-to-date armament and a few tanks, instead of spending so much to build up a public relations force for the minister, or to enlarge the scope of his headquarters by employing so many civilians to serve such a comparatively small number in the armed forces?
There is a definite right on the part of the taxpayer, and members of parliament on his behalf, to say, "yes, but". There have been many deficiencies and failings in the minister's discharge of his responsibility for the adequate preparation of our defences, but none so glaring as his totally unjustified assumption of omniscience and superiority in his condemnation of any possible criticism before it had even been voiced. We are dealing here with a proposed expenditure of $2,000 million, and yet the minister says: Do not criticize or attempt to show that we are doing anything wrong or that anything we are doing should be done in a different way; to do so will be merely showing hindsight.
The very fact that we have so tragically little in the way of forces in being at this moment and are proposing to spend this vast amount extra and will still have only very limited increases in our available striking force by the end of the year constitutes the strongest possible condemnation and criticism of the defence program of which the minister is in nominal charge. The whole situation with which we are confronted indicates to my mind that the minister, far from adopting this perverted attitude in connection with his relationship to the House of Commons and the country, should instead be inviting not only the house but the country to take a second look at defence; should be

explaining why after having spent $2,500 million in the last two years there is virtually nothing to show for it, and why we are being asked to authorize another $2,000 million. Up to date we have had little in the way of concrete information as to what we are going to have in being at the end of this year.
I believe that the whole situation calls for a total reassessment of our defence effort and a far greater concentration on the preparing of our forces in Canada with equipment and weapons which have some relation to reality and to the necessary state of preparedness and equipment to meet and to beat the only foe we shall ever be called upon to fight.

Mr. Speaker, as one who had the privilege of serving in two world wars I am naturally interested in all matters pertaining to defence. Today I should like to draw attention to one aspect of national defence which in my opinion is of vital importance. Last Thursday the minister placed on Hansard, at page 1084, an estimate of the enemy's strength. One hundred and seventy-five active Russian divisions represent 2,800,000 men whom Russia now has under arms, and one-third of these are mechanized. On mobilization this number could be doubled. We are informed from various sources that Russia has about 25,000 tanks, 20,000 aircraft and 350 submarines. In addition she is feverishly rearming her satellites, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Roumania, Bulgaria and Hungary.
The question naturally arises: For what purpose has this overwhelmingly powerful force been built up? Certainly it is not to protect Russia against any possible aggressor. The Kremlin knows full well that there is no nation in the world today that wishes or is likely to wish to invade Russia. To find the answer we must examine the idea that dominates the rulers and people of Russia; the idea which determines everything they think, say and do; the idea which controls every phase of their national life, even their music. That idea was born 100 years ago in the mind of Karl Marx. Professor Theophil Spoerri, of Zurich university, has analysed it in these words:
With the communist manifesto (1848) comes the first expression of a new ideology: Marxism. Marxism would never have been so powerful if it did not arise out of reality. Marx's primary concern was man himself. "To be radical means to grasp the matter by the roots. For mankind those roots are man himself." Marx showed how through the economics of capital man himself became a thing. The worker sold his strength and time as goods. Thus work becomes the cause of alienation, divided personality. In this way being becomes materialistic.
Against this process of making things out of man, out of society, and out of nature, Marxism directs three positive basic principles. First, the "Praxis"

(practical program). "Philosophers have interpreted the world. The point is to change it." That is not only a challenge to action. It is a new philosophy: truth is only found in action . . . Secondly, the "Kommune,"-society. Man is not a private individual. He is a social creature. He becomes real only in relationship to other men. The goal of history is to do away with the barriers between men and classes: the "classless society." Thirdly, the "Totale," the whole. In this faith in a new order of society there lies an unconscious religious element. Through Karl Marx the Jewish Messianic creed has permeated the modern labour movement. It is in the sense of the whole (the "dialectic movement,"-through opposites towards a synthesis), that every individual finds his rights, all divisions are cured and all fixations broken.
In political terms this idea is described as a "people's" democracy to distinguish it from our "western" democracy. This "people's" democracy offers social justice, order, discipline and equality-but at a price; the price of tyranny and a brutal and ruthless suppression of the individual for the benefit of the masses. A former communist has summed up the religious aspects of communism in the words, "A vision of man without God." It is a system which denies the existence of God. It sets up the state as the supreme authority and forces man to live for society and not for himself. In social terms it is a force that transcends all frontiers and all barriers of class, wealth, race or colour. An ex-communist describes this force as follows:
Communists are bound together by no secret oath. The tie that binds them across the frontiers of nations, across barriers of language and differences of class and education, in defiance of religion, morality, truth, law, honour, the weaknesses of the body and the irresolutions of the mind, even unto death, is a simple conviction:	It is necessary
now to change the world. Their power, whose nature baffles the rest of the world, because in a large measure the rest of the world has lost that power, is the power to hold convictions and to act upon them.
The key then to the whole communist philosophy lies in these words: "It is necessary to change the world", to change it by every means available, economic, political, psychological; by peaceful means if possible but by force if necessary. This then is the reason and purpose for the huge Russian war machine; to change the world, to change the present system, to impose upon the world the communist way of life. We therefore have to meet two powerful forces, the Russian military might and the far more powerful communist ideology which it is meant to serve.
The Korean aggression alerted us to our real danger. Last Thursday the minister reported the progress we have made in building up our forces and our plans for the current fiscal year. A few days ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) brought us up to date on NATO; and this, together with reports from the 55704-79
National Defence
United Nations, indicates that on the political front we are holding our own and have even made some advances. The taxes we have to pay remind us continually of the efforts that are being made on the economic front, and we are well aware of the great advantages we enjoy on the industrial front by reason of our great natural wealth and our industrial potential.
But it is the ideological front with which I am concerned today. This is the most important front of all. The battle goes on continuously without ceasing and it is a struggle for survival. The Christian idea of man as a creature of God and the communist idea of man without God cannot exist side by side in the same world. The struggle must go on until one or the other triumphs. Success on other fronts cannot result in a lasting peace. The best it can produce is an armed truce in which the cold war will continue as fiercely as ever, with endless taxes and endless money and energy being poured into non-productive channels instead of being used to serve the needs of humanity.
On the other hand, if we win the war of ideas we cannot possibly lose on any other front, and lasting peace and all those other things for which our comrades fought and died in two world wars will be assured.
A great European scholar, Professor Eiliv Skard, dean of the faculty of humanities of Oslo university, has this to say:
We live in an ideological age. I think it is necessary to stress it. The man who is not clear on that fact does not really understand his time. We know from the history of the last years that a nation with a false ideology can ruin the world, and we know that a nation without an ideology will go down.
We have, Mr. Speaker, two enemies, the Russian military might and the communist ideology. We can meet military power with military power. We can match economic force with economic force. We can check political moves with political counter-moves. But no military, political or economic force can defeat an idea. An idea can only be conquered by a better idea, an ideology only by a superior ideology.	.
Do we have such an idea? Can we develop a superior ideology? The answer is yes. We in the western democracies are a little shy and timid when it comes to talking about ideologies. We almost feel it is a sign of weakness even to mention the word, so we try to meet the passion and plan of alien ideologies with talk, with lip service to high ideals, and as a last recourse with force. Then we hope to live on as we have always lived, selfishly, comfortably and undisturbed. The truth is that we do have a superior ideology.

National Defence
The Christian idea with its moral and spiritual values, upon which our western democracy is based, is far superior to the communist idea and far more radical and revolutionary. Communism does not go to the root of the trouble, because it seeks only to change the system. The Christian idea goes further; it seeks to change man himself.
The claim is made on every hand that human nature cannot be changed. That is the big lie of our time. It is the lie on which communism bases its justification for the class struggle. It is the lie behind which we hide when we are unwilling to change. It is a lie that has been disproved over and over again in the history of the Christian religion and is being disproved by overwhelming evidence around us every day.
We do have a superior idea capable of developing unity between people of every race, class, colour and nation. It is the Christian idea, which is the very foundation of our democratic way of life. The thing to do, as my colleague from Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) has pointed out, is to live it; because only if we live it can it achieve its full force and vitality.
Last Thursday the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) stated that NATO represented a new concept in international co-operation and organization. We are a partnership of free nations bound together by a common danger represented by a common enemy. That concept will become much more meaningful, however, and the partnership far stronger when the countries of NATO are bound together by a common ideology based on a common set of moral and spiritual values. Only then will we be equipped to move from a partnership of fear to a partnership of faith when the common danger is surmounted. It has been said in this house that our policy is one of peace through strength. No nation is strong that is ideologically weak; and it has been demonstrated that the strongest army cannot long defend a weak ideology.
Russia has mastered and perfected the art of ideological warfare. So skilful has she become in applying this new war strategy that already she has conquered eight nations of eastern Europe and gained the alliance of a large part of Asia without employing a single soldier and without firing a single shot. Today in every nation of the world communist agents full of zeal for their cause are busy undermining the nations from within so they will fall an easy prey to the communist idea. We know how these agents work, how they use propaganda to spread fear, confuse issues and undermine confidence in our national leaders; how they mobilize the negative forces of fear, greed, hate, resentment, suspicion, fMr. Carter.]
lust, pride, ambition and selfishness; how they seek by every means to weaken and destroy a nation's morals.
How else can we meet this threat, unless we begin at once to build up our ideological defences, to forge ideological weapons and learn to fight ideologically, as Russia does? Doubtless that was what General Eisenhower had in mind in the paragraph to which the minister called particular attention at page 1083 of Hansard, and which I repeat:
The momentum must be continued with renewed vigour, and since moral force is the genesis of all progress, especially progress towards security and peace, we must give primary attention to this vital element.
In his address to the senate foreign relations committee in Paris last July General Eisenhower had this to say:
The one thing I want to stress at the beginning is this: the struggle going on in the world is for the minds and hearts of men. It is an ideological struggle. There is every possible way of going about the thing, and open warfare is only one method.
No one can escape the ideological war. It is total war. It involves both civilians and the armed forces. Everyone needs ideological training. It has to start somewhere, and in my opinion the logical place to start is with the armed services, for these reasons. They have the organizational framework in which such training can be carried out immediately. Secondly, it is a weapon of definite value in battle, since soldiers inspired and moved by the fire and zeal of a militant ideology have a definite advantage over those who are not. I think this has been proved by the fanaticism and determination shown by the communist troops in Korea. Besides all this, should a war break out between the communist countries and the democracies, even if the democracies secured a military victory, what then? Can the democracies police Asia? Can they feed the teeming, hungry millions of India and Asia? If not, what is the answer? Surely the solution lies in giving them an idea bigger and better than communism to live for and be governed by.
Our armed forces are the ambassadors of the democracies among the people of the nations where they are serving. By their conduct they interpret democracy to those people, and if they give an adequate demonstration of the democratic way of life there is no doubt that this idea will capture the hearts and minds of the people among whom our forces are serving.
I think we have been somewhat reticent in facing realistically the need for ideological training for our forces because the armies of the communist world have attached so much importance to it. It is their daily fare,

completely integrated with their training in arms. We have tended to regard it with the distaste we feel for propaganda, a distaste that has been developed by the communist prostitution of that fundamentally decent word and procedure. However, we cannot afford the luxury of self-righteousness or oversensitivity in this respect. The attack is real, the weapons are real, and the techniques are real. It is an attack launched and maintained by trained men. We may hate the intent and its methods but to ignore either is to court disaster.
I should like to commend the step taken last year when the bureau of current affairs was set up for the Canadian armed forces, to help the serviceman determine that which he had enlisted to support and that which he must be prepared to oppose. As an initial step it was excellent. By introducing discussion group techniques it has enabled a trial and error experiment to be carried out which by this time should have established what problems have to be overcome, what methods are most effective and exactly what is required to achieve the objectives announced by the minister last year.
I had a great deal of experience with this kind of work in world war II and also in adult education in civil life, and for that reason I have had a special interest in the B.C.A. program. I know from my own experience and from the experience of my opposite numbers in the United States forces during the last war how difficult it is to get area and command headquarters to support such programs on their own initiative. I know how difficult it is for the young junior officer to initiate such a program without some special training, without proper accommodation and without other physical requirements essential to its implementation. I understand the reaction of the officer who regards it as just one more chore for which he is Joe. I know how easy it is for those who are hostile to the program to sabotage it, and discredit it as somebody or other's special pet whim. Finally, I realize the danger that negative and subversive elements may take advantage of it to defeat it and deflect it from its true purpose.
I should like to see the B.C.A. program integrated with other training programs. I should like to see adequate provision for training schedules, and the means of implementation in various formations authorized by national defence headquarters. I should like to see training schools and short courses for selected officers who are to implement the program, just as is given in the case of gas warfare, guided missiles and any other specialized arm. From my own experience, 55704-79J

I know that mere information, in itself, is not sufficient. Academic discussion of topics, however timely, however interesting, is not enough. This has been proven over and over again by the discussions under ABCA in the British army, and the even more elaborate information and educational program of the United States army. To be effective for ideological training, the information must have ideological content, and both the information and discussion must be geared to ideological objectives. It is also essential that men giving leadership in this program are themselves convinced that we have the superior ideology.
In order that there be no misunderstanding, I should like to list what I consider to be some of the main objectives of an ideological training program:
1.	To give personnel a vision of what inspired democracy really is-a vision of mankind working out its destiny under the guidance of God.
2.	To give personnel a clear understanding of the moral and spiritual truths upon which this vision of inspired democracy is founded, which has given it strength in the past and upon which its future survival depends.
3.	To develop a fighting faith in an idea far bigger than man himself, an idea which will satisfy all their inner longings and aspirations and to which they can give themselves completely and fully. That is what communism does for communists.
4.	To train personnel to be ideologically minded; to be able to discern the ideological battlelines that run through all the issues and problems of our present day, whether in politics, business, industry or in the home.
5.	To enable personnel to recognize the ideological content of communist propaganda whether spoken, written or printed and to meet it with a counter ideology.
6.	To recognize material with ideological content and sources of such material.
7.	To give personnel basic knowledge of the nature of alien ideologies and their fundamental principles.
8.	To train personnel to recognize the ideological weapons and tactics used by the enemy, and to develop counter weapons and tactics for democracy.
9.	To enable personnel to understand
clearly in simple positive terms exactly what Canada is fighting for, and what we are fighting against. To say we are fighting for the four freedoms or against aggression is not sufficient.	.
It should be obvious that mere information and academic discussions cannot achieve any

National Defence
of these objectives, because ideological training affects the heart and will as much as the mind and intellect. I hope the minister will find it possible to give some consideration to these suggestions, because much of this kind of training need not cost the taxpayers one extra cent and the total cost is comparably insignificant. Without it, we cannot achieve maximum effectiveness of our efforts in other directions. With it, we cannot possibly lose. It is an iron-clad guarantee of total victory and lasting peace with minimum cost and effort.
I realize that there are difficulties. I realize that Canada, in military terms, is a small country, but a small country with a big idea can change the history of the world. Napoleon said that there are only two powers in the world, the sword and the spirit. In the long run, the sword is always defeated by the spirit. This dictum so applicable in Napoleon's time is even more pertinent today when the enemy is communist ideology as well as Russian military power.
. Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence): Mr. Speaker, this is not a substantive motion and I understand that consequently I have no right of reply. A number of questions have been asked, and if it were to meet the wishes of hon. members I would be glad to try to answer them.
Agreed.

In the course of the debate which has taken place a number of members have dealt with the same matters, and I have tried to collect their comments under as small A number of headings as possible. Perhaps the point that was made most often by members of the opposition groups was that our 27th infantry brigade in Europe should be an armoured brigade. To this, other assertions were added, such as those made by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) that we have not got a scrap of armour, not an operational tank and so on. It was suggested also that we should have built tanks in Canada. These points of view are serious, and I believe have largely been dealt with by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. George) in his Speech last Friday night.
i There are additional points I should mention. This 27th Canadian brigade was announced for the first time in this house on fday 4, 1951, when its composition was announced. The next day there appeared in the newspapers a full page advertisement for the 27th Canadian infantry brigade group. That was eleven months ago. At that time the house was in session and there were many opportunities, including nine days spent' on the estimates, when anyone who was critical
fMr. Carter.]
of the organization of this brigade might have raised his voice. Then we had a fall session. During that session the question of defence was discussed on the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on October 22. While I do not suggest that the approval of that resolution by the house without a dissenting voice meant that the house approved everything the government had done, I do suggest it presented an opportunity for any hon. member who felt that something had not been done correctly to say so.
It was not, however, until the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) spoke on the radio program "The Nation's Business" in January that this suggestion was made. Long before that time this brigade had been equipped, trained and transported to Germany where it was stationed. If this suggestion was intended to be placed before the government in time for it to take effective action, it was too late. I think there appears to be a good deal of misunderstanding about the composition of an infantry brigade group. This term does not apply to any fixed set of formations, but generally speaking it is taken to mean a formation which includes three infantry battalions, an artillery regiment, a tank squadron and all the other formations necessary to enable that group to operate as an independent unit. It was that type of organization we created to send to Korea, where it has been found that its general balance of arms and of formations has met the need admirably. No other formation has a better record. The composition of the various formations has been the subject of continuous examination not only by the officers of our own armed forces but also by those of other forces. So far as I know, it has not been suggested by anyone in a responsible position we followed the wrong course either as to weapons or organization.
One of the newspapers said that this brigade "consists of foot-soldiers, the PBI, in army parlance, each man equipped with a rifle and nothing more". The fact is that only 40 per cent of the men are armed only with rifles. The rest have mortars, machine guns, 25-pounders, anti-tank weapons, rocket launchers, flame-throwers and, finally, tanks. As I say, the composition is designed to enable the brigade to train and fight alone or in association with larger formations.
The 27th Canadian infantry brigade group is practically identical in composition with the 25th brigade groups. It has tanks. The armoured unit in Europe is equipped with Centurions which we have bought from Britain, whereas in Korea we are using the No. IV, which is the latest model of the

Sherman which we bought from the United States. In Europe our brigade is operating as an independent brigade; it is not formed into any division or corps. It is training as an individual brigade; and it is planned to establish it in its own training area towards the end of this year.
An armoured brigade group is a new term, I think. We know of armoured brigades-
We had them in the last war.
An armoured brigade group of the type such as I have mentioned, which can operate independently? I am informed that one has never been formed.
We had two of them in the Canadian army.

We had an armoured brigade, as I understand it, namely, a brigade of armour which was not designed to operate separately but rather was designed to operate with one or more divisions. The establishment that I have been given to enable an armoured brigade to constitute an independent armoured brigade group operating separately would be, by a good many hundreds of men, a larger establishment than the one for the Canadian infantry brigade group. In other words, the suggestion that this procedure would save men is entirely ill-founded. It would take more men to operate this brigade group as an armoured brigade group than to operate it as an infantry brigade group.
I think the suggestion was that it would save men by establishing more efficient use of men.
The suggestion was made that it would save men.
That was not the main import of the suggestion.

Well, it was said. I do not know whether it was what was meant. The suggestion was made too that we should send not troops but technicians.
The next point I want to make is that it was never suggested to us that we should send an armoured brigade group. In fact the contrary suggestion was made.
We have been acquiring tanks from the British at the fastest rate they could deliver them to us. We have now received delivery of over 40. Some of them are in Europe and the rest are in Canada. We shall be taking more on an order which is well over 200. We are taking them as fast as we can secure them.

Are those all Centurions?

Yes. I do not believe it would have been possible to get Centurions before we got those that were delivered to us. Certainly it would not have been possible for us to manufacture Centurions in Canada, before the first Centurions were delivered to us inasmuch as they had not reached the stage, even in England, where production.' could have been commenced in Canada and developed to the point where there would be* actual delivery. From the point of view of time, I am informed by the Department of Defence Production that there is nothing in* that suggestion, that we are getting Centurions as fast as we could, and that we are getting them in as large numbers as we can.

We would also find' ourselves equipped with all the tanks we: could possibly conceive of our needing in' another world war, should it come; then the productive capacity would be idle and we' would find ourselves with an aging group of* obsolescent tanks and faced, at some stage or another, with the necessity of repeating the operation five, six or seven years later.
Mr' Fulton: 1 am sorry to interrupt, but if the minister will permit me to do so, may I. say that I am sure he will admit that the: suggestion was never confined explicitly to manufacturing tanks only for Canada. It was rather to manufacture tanks on the same; basis as that on which we are now manufac-s turing the F-86E, namely, for ourselves and. for our allies.
To give them away?
I do not understand we are giving away the F-86E.

Yes, every one of them; that is, to Britain. We have indicated what we propose to give away, and what we propose to give away are the types of equipment that we ourselves need and that other countries need, which are not being manufactured in sufficient quantities by other countries and which we have the special facilities to produce-for example, the gun plant at Sorel or Longueuil-whereas a tank factory would require entirely new facilities.
Finally, may I say that there are two additional reasons why it makes sense for us to purchase Centurion tanks. One is that, by placing this order in Britain, we enable the British to build up a production line and that enables them to produce larger numbers of tanks at lower costs, a result that is greatly to be

desired from the point of view of over-all defence planning. It also helps to give economic assistance to the British by reason of the fact that we pay them for what we get, including these tanks.
As to -the equipment that we have ordered from the United States, we ordered tanks- Pattons and others-but it has been found necessary to make substantial modifications in those types, and they will not be in production by the time we hope to have delivery of the Centurions which have proved themselves to be good tanks in battle in Korea.
. With regard to other types of equipment which we were going to acquire from the United States, there have been delays; but surely hon. members were not surprised at the fact that there should be delays when they recall what happened in Korea after the orders were placed. Delivery had been commenced in respect of equipment we had ordered and which was to be delivered to us; but it was found that it was more urgently needed somewhere else. We had equipment to meet our own needs, both in Europe and here, and it made sense that the United States type of equipment we bad ordered from that country should be used for other purposes.
Referring to the air carrier, hon. members have suggested that we should modernize the Magnificent, or get more of them. Magnificent in its present condition is a carrier of a type still in current use in the Royal Navy. There is in process a procedure of modernization, refitting and the like; and when its turn comes Magnificent will be exposed to that procedure. That is taking place in accordance with arrangements which have been worked out with the Royal Navy.
We have considered adding another carrier to our navy, but it would mean giving up something else, or getting more money- because we cannot use the defence dollar twice. The operation of carriers is a large-scale business. There are only four countries on our side, so far as I know, which have carriers-the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and ourselves. And the number is not very great. However there are some in reserve. We feel it very desirable that we should have one carrier for training or operations, on anti-submarine activities; but to have two of them would be a pretty considerable undertaking for us in peacetime.
As our role is largely anti-submarine, the Avenger aircraft, with which our carrier is fitted, are very suitable for this purpose, and will probably continue for some time to be more suitable than any jet yet in sight for anti-submarine work. Jets, which have a

short range, a high landing speed and not a very high load-carrying capacity, are not considered yet as suitable entirely for the purpose. It is not expected therefore that for this purpose jets will come into active operation until some time in the fairly distant future.
Questions were asked about the progress of the CF-100. The CF-100 and the Orenda engine were started late in 1946. Detailed design was commenced in the middle of 1947, and the first prototype was flown in January, 1950. That is about three years after the start, which is considered good time for the first flight of a new type of aircraft. The tests both of the engine on the ground and of the aircraft and engine in the air proved satisfactory. As I have said before, both the manufacturer and the R.C.A.F. felt that they would be in production much faster than is the normal time for the development of a new type of aircraft. It turns out that it is not much faster, but about the same as is usual for similar types of aircraft of a totally new design. The CF-100 pre-production order is well on the way to completion now, with several aircraft about ready to be delivered. I saw them two weeks ago in Toronto. The engine plant will begin production on a regular production-line basis in June. It will be at half 'the planned rate in September, and running at the full planned rate in 1953.
I expect we will be producing enough Orenda engines to enable us to begin using them in the F-86E early in 1953. That engine will give the F-86E still more speed than it has today-and it is generally recognized as the fastest aircraft there is.
The next point mentioned was with regard to standardization. I did not say anything about it in my introductory remarks, because there have been no major developments. There is steady progress at the working level, working out the specifications and, in some oases, the design for equipment. A good many kinds of procedures and types of equipment have been standardized but the situation with regard to the rifle remains much as it was.
Following the meeting of defence ministers of the United States, France, Great Britain and Canada in Washington last year, we agreed to refer the matter to the standing group. The committee appointed by the standing group made a report to the meeting of defence ministers at the North Atlantic council. That report was considered, and was the subject of discussion between Mr. Churchill and myself in London in November, and here in January, in the course of which he told me that they had decided not to go into all-out production of the .280, but to

continue development work looking toward production at a date some time in the future.
Meanwhile the United States has said it will not be ready to change from the Garand .300 for several years. That is the situation. We have rifles of the .303 No. IV which are being used by our troops in Korea, and are still found satisfactory as the .303 always was. Our troops in Europe are also equipped with the .303. We have considerable numbers of .303's in Canada, and also of Garands. We do not propose to go into production of rifles until the situation becomes clearer. We have enough rifles to see us through the first year of a war. We have good production equipment, could go into production and reach a high rate within a short time so as to produce rifles for ourselves and our allies to meet our needs, and to assist in meeting theirs.
The suggestion was made that we are short of equipment in Canada. For example, take 25-pounders. We have all the 25-pounders we need. We have given away several hundred, and we will continue to keep the rest until we acquire the 105 millimetres, which we are going to produce in Canada, as well as the 155.
A question was asked also about the situation regarding anti-aircraft guns. It was said that we had given away all our anti-aircraft guns, and that we are doing nothing about it. We gave away one hundred 3.7 guns and replaced them by one hundred 90 millimetre guns acquired from the United States. We have more on order from the United States and we have a still larger number of 3.7's in our own possession in Canada. When we get the guns from the United States we shall probably release further guns to Europe.
I was asked to give some figures on construction. The 1952-53 program includes a carry-over from 1951-52 of $198 million. This represents contracts which have been let and which we expect to complete in 1952-53. The program for 1952-53 provides for an additional $46 million of contracts to be completed this year.
As I explained, this construction is required by reason of the greatly increased size of the armed forces and increased operations. We will have to carry on a construction program of somewhat this magnitude for several years yet before we have the accommodation and training and operational facilities needed for our forces as presently planned.
Reference was made to the number of civilians in the armed forces. Our position on this has been made clear on a number of occasions. The policy is to use a civilian in place of service personnel in every case
National Defence
where it would be possible to use a civilian in wartime. If we have a stenographer or telegrapher or clerk at national defence headquarters and do not need to have that person in uniform in war, then we employ a civilian.
The figure of 40,000 civilians which I gave includes both classified and prevailing rates. The actual number at February 28, was 39,398, of which 20,093 are classified and 19,305 prevailing rates employees. The latter figure includes some 5,000 casual workers who are engaged at camps and the like for short periods. The figure of 19,305 prevailing rates employees covers workers engaged in the dockyards, in the shops, at camps and so on, just as if they were employed by an ordinary employer. They receive the rates of wages prevailing in the locality for their types of work.
Since Korea, where the strength of the armed forces has increased 100 per cent, from 47,000 to 95,300, the strength of civilian employees has not gone up anything like that amount. Further, the number of service personnel at national defence headquarters has only increased by 255 or 12 per cent since Korea, whereas the total strength of the armed forces has increased by 100 per cent. These figures can be better examined when we get into a detailed discussion of the estimates. I assure hon. members that this question of the size of the armed forces and the way in which they are employed is receiving continuous consideration at every possible level.
We can say, and I have said before, that applying the same standards to the forces of other countries, our forces are equally operational or even more so. For example, over forty per cent of the men in the navy are at sea; our fliers have more hours of flying per month for each man on the strength of the air force, and that kind of thing. We are not satisfied merely to compare our standards with those of other countries and we must continue to do increasingly better in every respect.
The next point mentioned was that of obsolescent equipment, having regard I understood particularly to aircraft. We are going to replace obsolete equipment as fast as we can with better equipment. We are producing the F-86E at a rate which compares favourably with production in the United States. We expect to be able to meet our commitments for deliveries to the United States and to Great Britain and to equip our own twelve squadrons as well as the necessary reserves. We expect to be doing the same with the CF-100, using it for the defence of Canada. As the CF-100 comes

National Defence
into operation it will be issued to the squadrons, both active and auxiliary, which may be using Mustangs or Mitchells.
However, both the Mustang and the Mitchell have been found to be exceedingly rugged and useful aircraft right up to the present time. They would be very useful in connection with the kind of operation that might have to be engaged in should we be attacked in the near future. The Mustang has a range and speed which makes it well able to take on the type of bomber which might reach Canada according to our present information.
With regard to Harvards, our production rate is substantial and able to meet our requirements. We are not going to produce quite as many Harvards as we at first planned, but we will be producing more of the new jet plane, the T-33, which is the modern version of the P-81.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Dinsdale) referred to the armament of the F-86. As he understands, the question of aircraft armament is highly controversial. It is also one that is much easier to discuss with the technicians. As I have told him, they will be available at any time. The situation as it has been explained to me is this: About a year ago it was felt that the F-86E should be equipped with a gun larger than the 50 calibre. Long before that research and development work had been going on with various types of 20-calibre guns and rockets. However, the record still speaks for itself and indicates that the armament of the F-86E is still adequate to shoot down far more MiG's than the reverse.
The MIG-15 has three heavier guns, but they have a slower rate of fire and a much lower muzzle velocity. Therefore their lethal quality is quite different from that of the F-86E. In the hands of a good gunner the latter appears to be the better equipment.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) referred to wastage and he mentioned a figure of 15,279 wastage as compared with an intake of 41,757. I would submit that statistically the correct operation is to relate wastage to the total strength. If you do that you get a figure of about 15 per cent which compares favourably with any figure we had during the second world war or in the period between world wars. Except in so far as it reduces the number of trained officers and tradesmen, wastage is one way of developing trained reserves. In countries which have compulsory military training of eighteen months or two years you have a very large proportion of the total trained personnel going back to civilian life every year. On a

two-year basis 50 per cent will go back every year, and that is considered a part of the normal operation of building up trained personnel who act as a reserve. In Canada we have had 26,000 officers and men leave the armed forces since the end of the second world war, and a very considerable proportion of them are available for service in the event of an emergency.
The hon. member, at page 1130 of Hansard, referred to the situation at Claresholm, where he said:
Apparently the housing situation was bad; houses were needed, so they sent in a whole bunch of metal prefabricated units. They came in and were put on a siding before the contracts had been let for their erection or for the plumbing, wiring and so on. As a result there was no one to unload them, so special people had to be hired to do that job.
Then he said a little later:
So they sent a bunch of people to load these prefabricated houses on railway cars and ship them out; then they started all over again. I do not know where those houses have gone, but I have been led to believe I would not be far wrong if I said they may be in England at the present time. How much money was lost in that deal I do not know, but it must have been many thousands of dollars.
The fact is that 150 prefabricated houses were ordered and delivered in January in accordance with the order on the site at Claresholm. Tenders were called by Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation for the erection of the houses this spring with the beginning of the building season. The contract was awarded ten days ago. The contractor is on the job and about to start work. None of these houses has been taken anywhere. There is nothing whatever in the story.
The hon. member also referred to the question of reserves. I mentioned the total strength of the reserves as being 58,000. We have had really remarkable support of the active forces from the reserves during the year. Over 5,000 members of the reserve forces have gone active duing the year 195152. Despite that the number of the reserves has increased, and despite the loss of what must have been some of their most active and enthusiastic members the amount of training done during the summer months was about the same as the year before. About 11,000 personnel engaged in summer training.
The reserves have a role which has been explained so many times in the house that there is no need for me to enlarge on it. I have referred repeatedly to the really great contribution they make by devoting part of their time to the service of Canada. It was on the base of the reserve forces that the Canadian forces in the great war of 1914-18 and

the second world war were built up. We are in a different position now with many more forces in being than we had before either of the two world wars.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) referred to batmen. Batmen are provided only for single men living in barracks or camps and the scale is one to four junior officers. Only in the case of officers of the rank of colonel or above living in married quarters is a servant allowed.
The hon. member referred to men joining the reserve forces as athletes. I would be glad if he would bring such cases to my attention. I have heard about this matter from time to time. It is strictly against the regulations and the practice, but if it happens, we will take action.
Then he referred to a situation I could not quite place but I rather took from what he said that he had reference to Kildare barracks on Laurier avenue. The squatters were put out of there a year ago and it was occupied as single men's quarters. A complaint was made by people in the neighbourhood that we had these soldiers living there and there were no curtains or blinds. So blinds were installed long before the provost corps moved into the building, and it is now occupied by three officers and thirty-six men.
A question was raised as to education in the armed forces, and in that connection I might refer the hon. member to the answer given in the house to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) on the 20th of November, 1951. Provision is made for the education of members of the armed forces. It is done under the same system as that under which the Canadian Legion educational services operated during the war. The same material is used, but instead of using Legion personnel, who were paid by the Department of National Defence during the war, we now use Department of Veterans Affairs personnel who are paid by the Department of National Defence. In addition, we have educational officers with the units and they have staffs who distribute literature about the courses, make books available, collect papers, forward them to the Department of Veterans Affairs for correction, and so on. It is the same arrangement we had during the war.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) referred to the bureau of current affairs. It is working well. Training courses have been given already for officers who are assigned to lead their men in discussion groups and the like, and periods of as much as an hour a week are provided for that activity.
