Mr. Speaker, as is customary I wish to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for the clear and interesting picture he has given of our affairs. I not only wish to thank him;
I wish to say that I welcome seeing in what he has said certain signs of repentance. That give me great satisfaction. I know the minister will not expect me to go further than he went himself in praising him. In fact I do not know that there is anything I can add to that except to say I should like to hear the minister when he is not in a modest mood. Certainly I can say this to the minister, that if I ever have an unpleasant and nasty pill which I wish gilded I would hope I might have his assistance in doing it. I was particularly interested in the joy registered by those who have applauded the minister. Their constituents must be very different from mine.
They are.

They evidently live in constituencies where people love high prices but in Greenwood as a matter of fact the people do not love high prices. I would ask these members if they have a formula to make the people in their constituencies like high prices will they disclose it to me, or still better, will they come and help me in Greenwood?
They like balanced budgets too.

As the minister was speaking of millions, hundreds of millions and billions I was thinking of a different kind of people, people who do not deal in billions or hundreds of millions and who, as a matter of fact, in spite of the success story we have heard tonight, in spite of the glowing figures we have heard tonight, do not find they are sharing very greatly in this prosperity. They feel that it is passing them by. They are unhappy and perplexed. It is about them I wish to talk tonight. They hear a lot about the glories of our currency. They hear much said about our dollar being at par with the United States dollar, but they know that our dollar is not at par with the things they have to buy, with bread, meat, milk and clothes. They know it is at a 50 per cent
discount with relation to those things, and that bothers them. As I say, they are bothered by high taxes and high prices, and recently they have begun to be bothered by unemployment too.
I should like to refer to certain things that are said by friends of the government in commenting on this situation but first I should like to say that so far as I can see the chickens are beginning to come home to roost, and they are not a very pleasant brood when you look at them. I think the people of Canada are going to look at them closely because one thing the minister has done-and in this he has had shining success-is that he has made the people of Canada tax conscious, tax puzzled and tax angry in a way that in my memory they have never been before. I think they will indeed welcome the suggestion of the mayor of Ottawa that in addition to a cost of living index there should be a cost of taxes index. All the soothing things that the minister says are not going to take their minds away from these things.
I come now to the amount that we are being asked to raise, and I should like to read a brief statement from the Winnipeg Free Press which, in spite of occasional qualms, supports this government through thick and thin. What has it got to say about the figure of $4,335 million plus, plus, plus, about which I will say something in a moment? The Free Press of March 22, 1952, has this to say:
These figures will enable the public, all of whom in one or other form are taxpayers, to realize the disturbing and, indeed, appalling way in which federal expenditures have risen in recent years.
The Free Press later refers to government profligacy, and I shall refer to it too. The Free Press is right. These figures are appalling. The minister has explained to us how he is going to deal with them this year, and if we continue on the crest of a rising boom he will deal with them this year and undoubtedly even have another surplus. Maybe we will find it tucked away somewhere. Nevertheless it is an appalling thing because to begin with we have $4,335 million. Then you can add $100 million right away to cover the dominion-provincial tax agreements. Then there was $441 million in supplementary estimates this year. On that basis

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell you would have $4,876 million, or say $4,800 million. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is $13,150,000 a day. It is $547,000 an hour and it is nearly $10,000 a minute. In other words, since I began to speak five minutes ago the minister has taken $50,000 out of our pockets.
Putting it differently, it comes to something like $343 for every man, woman and child on the average. I know that average figure is criticized but nevertheless it is a rough and ready guide. If you take a family of five it is $1,715 and that would come to about $30 a week in taxation. I admit that figure needs adjustment but it is a figure that people might just as well have in their minds. The minister takes it lightly and buoyantly. He speaks about buoyant revenues, and they are buoyant, although we must remind ourselves that they are produced very substantially by inflated prices. Sometimes I think the minister almost feels that taxes come like manna from heaven.
Last year we pointed out to the minister exactly what was going to happen if these extra taxes were imposed. On April 16, 1951, as found at page 2051 of Hansard I said:
This budget, which is purporting to cure inflation, will cause as its inescapable first result a substantial increase in the cost of living.
We told the minister that, and it was true. We told him it would produce a surplus beyond what he expected, and that was true. Notwithstanding the formidable words used by the minister, I propose to say a little about the mystery of the surplus. In the beginning I would say to the minister that if it were not so serious this matter of the surplus would be rather amusing. Indeed, in certain quarters they are dealing with it as if it had become a kind of joke, not a very good joke. The Montreal Gazette had an editorial this morning beginning, "Button, button, who's has got the button".
That is partly because of a broadcast the minister made on February 19 in which he referred to the then surplus of $722 million and went out of his way to say what a good thing it was that this unexpected surplus had arisen. In his radio address he had this to say:
Supposing we had not had this large budgetary surplus, where would we have got the money for all these necessary loans, advances and Investments?
I thought that was an odd thing because after all the minister had these requirements in his mind in April when he budgeted, but nevertheless that is what the minister said. As I say, he explained that these moneys had been spent, and indeed he rather gloried in it. I want to point out that these moneys were used for loans and investments without any warning to the people who paid the taxes that that was going to be done. I think there


is no question whatever that the people who paid the taxes would be in the highest degree surprised to find that their money had been used in this way. There is no other conclusion they could reach but that hundreds of millions of dollars were taken from them unnecessarily.
The situation in the public mind is well pictured by a cartoon I have here from the St. Catharines Standard. It depicts the minister-

speechtext: Put it on Hansard.

Unfortunately I have got to return it. On the whole it is not uncomplimentary at all. The minister looks firm and rather aggressive, but on the other hand he is depicted in this fashion. He is a conjuror on a platform. One can see a very interested spectator just below-there seems to be only one-and in his left hand the minister is holding up a rabbit which is inscribed "That embarrassing surplus." The minister is saying, "Now, watch this vanish." The caption at the top is "But they usually multiply." My own suggestion to the minister is that he should have this called "Abbott's rabbit", and have it set up in his room.
This surplus, this bad budgeting, was a joint effort. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) got more money than he expected, and the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) did not spend as much as he expected. I think they had better get together and see whether they cannot do a better job this time. I always thought the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) could spend an unlimited amount of money, but apparently he did not quite come through this time.
Now I want to come back for a moment to taxes, which are really our greatest national industry. The minister is in this fortunate position, that whereas other creditors may have to wait for their money the tax collector goes and gets his. The minister is going to get, let us say, $4,800 million. I would like to compare that for a moment with some other interesting figures in our national economy. In 1950-I could not get the 1951 figures-the manufacturing industry of this country produced goods to the value of $4,378 million. In other words the minister is going to spend more than the product of our entire manufacturing industry. In 1950 the industry of agriculture produced goods to the value of $1,792 million, only about one-third of what the minister is going to get. The people of this country should register in their minds the amount the minister is going to spend, for it raises this question which we should all keep before us. When we talk

about the gross national product, it will be found that a very large part of that results from government expenditure. We are coming back to something like the war conditions, when we all remember that the government spent so much.
Now I want to say just a word about the cost of living. The minister did not say as much about that as I thought he would. Perhaps he was being modest, or perhaps the small drop in the cost of living calls up unpleasant memories of the foot-and-mouth disease scandal which has cut off our meat producers from the United States. It may even call up memories of unemployment, which now is rampant to some extent and which undoubtedly has had something to do with the drop. But I want to be fair; there has been a drop of 2| points in food prices in the last month or two. I have tried to get the best figures possible from those who understand these matters, to show what that would mean to an average family. As far as I can make out it would mean .46 cent a meal saved, or just under half a cent a meal. So I want to bring that to the attention of the house.
The next question I want to ask is, do we need all this money? On that point I should like to read a few words, again from the Winnipeg Free Press of March 22, where they say:
But the weak spot in the federal government's policy (and it now assumes a most aggravated form) is that it does not obey its own rules. It gives good advice and sets a thoroughly bad example. In this allowing expenditures to get out of hand Ottawa has failed to measure up to its own standard of what is required in these times.
And this also:
When the figures are searched for an explanation of this profligacy, none is to be found.
The word "profligacy" as I understand it means wasteful extravagance, and that is the word used by the Free Press.
Now let us see what sign of economy there is. I observe one thing of interest. We sometimes complain that the government does not share responsibility with us, but this is one place where the minister is very anxious to share responsibility, and to evade it himself. He evades responsibility by saying that really this is our fault, and that we should be helping him. That is true enough: nevertheless this is a government responsibility.
Do we need all this money, this $4,800 million? The government tries to create the impression that it is all in defence and social security, and a great deal of it is; but as the Free Press is careful to point out, that is not a complete answer. When we come back to defence one or two things should 55704-83
The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell be said there, too. I am sure everyone in this house wishes to spend for defence what is necessary to secure our safety; but that is not to say this figure of $2,100 million which is waved in our faces is necessarily a rock-bottom figure. During the defence debate in this house searching criticisms have been made which would suggest that this two billion dollar figure may be greatly exaggerated, and that is where some saving may be made. Presumably this gentle improvement in the tax situation which we have seen tonight may be taken as a preliminary to what is going to happen next year, when of course it will be very necessary to have some sweetener available.
I want to draw attention to just two or three of the items one finds in the estimates for next year. In the first place there is a figure of $46 million for travel and removal. I should be quick to say that includes moving troops to Korea and Germany; nevertheless $46 million is a lot of money and it is not possible for me to believe that something could not be done there. The next item I wish to refer to is $17 million for publicity. We all know what publicity is, of various kinds. It includes press hand-outs, films and all sorts of things; and I should point out that this amount does not include the salaries of that noble army who work in the various departments on publicity duties. This is merely what you might call out of pocket expenses.
A further figure, though it is not so large, which staggered me perhaps more than any other is an item of $4,891,000 in the defence department for telegraphs, telephones and other communications. I had a little illustration the other day which perhaps helps to explain that. A man who had been in the department years ago went in to obtain some information from an officer there. The officer said, "I don't know, but I will get it for you very quickly," and/ he reached for the telephone and telephoned to Vancouver. He did get the information very quickly. In these days of air mail I wonder if it is really so that there are urgent communications passing between the various officials of the government which require an expenditure of $4,891,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to comment briefly on the tax changes announced tonight. I welcome, as others will, the change in the corporation tax, though I regret very much it is still over 50 per cent which the minister has already stated more than once in this house he thinks too high. The relief is very little. It is rather like the hangman who, before the execution, offers you a cigarette. Still it is better than nothing, though not very

The Budget-Mr. J. M. Macdonnell much. We also welcome the minister's intention to try to help the utility companies, and I appreciate the fact that crown corporations are now going to pay their shot. On the personal income tax side, the correction of the inequity of having taxes running over 100 per cent was clearly called for. I think the minister's adjustments there will merit consideration, and presumably they will be a relief.
In connection with the sales tax it seems to me we find the minister not at his best. We find him here unrepentant and what I can only term perverse. It seems to me his pride is involved. He made statements last year with regard to the sales tax which we told him were wrong and which I submit in this last year have been abundantly proved wrong; nevertheless the minister persists. In connection with the excise tax I have already read to the house what we said last year; and I am glad to see that in this instance the minister has repented and that there is to be an adjustment. As to cigarettes, of course everyone knew that situation was impossible, but it is a pity that it had to be left to smugglers and bootleggers to correct it rather than those of us who regard ourselves as more respectable.
Why?

I am sure that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will agree with that anyway.
The minister has talked in billions to taxpayers who have to think in small amounts of five's and ten's. I believe he overlooked the fact that there are hundreds of thousands of voters in this country to whom his tax burden is a grievous one. They will feel again that, with this flood of expenditure, quite possibly, in spite of the check at the moment, prices may go up again if the spending develops in a big way, and that they may again be the victims of an unexpected surplus. They will certainly be on the lookout to see whether the situation arises in the coming year which they feel has arisen in the past year when they have been taxed) to an amount far beyond what was necessary.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT SAN FRANCISCO SEPTEMBER 8, 1951

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT SAN FRANCISCO SEPTEMBER 8, 1951
speechtext:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the treaty of peace with Japan, declarations (2) of Japan and Protocol, all as signed at San Francisco on the eighth day of September, 1951, and that this house do approve the same.
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1

He said: This motion which I have the honour to move gives to the house an opportunity to express its views on the Japanese peace treaty which was signed last autumn. The adoption of this resolution, which I think will commend itself to all sections of the house, will make it possible to bring the state of war with Japan to an end. I devoted some attention to this treaty, Mr. Speaker, in my remarks in the house on October 22 last, and at this time I do not want to repeat what I said then.
Since the signature of the treaty, it has been ratified by the Japanese Diet with the resounding vote of 307 to 47 recorded in the Japanese house of representatives. The United Kingdom government has also ratified the treaty-and deposited its instrument of ratification-as has the United States government. Parliamentary action has also been completed in Australia, New Zealand, Pakistan and Ceylon. The treaty will come into effect when a majority of eleven states, mentioned specifically in the treaty-a group which includes Canada-have ratified it. It seems likely, therefore, from the action which has been taken up to this moment, that the treaty will come into effect in the near future. This could happen whether or not Canada ratifies the treaty. I believe that no useful purpose would be served by this house delaying action in regard to the treaty at this time.
The treaty is a generous one. It has been represented by one of its main architects as a treaty of reconciliation, and that, I think, is what it is. Last October, when we were discussing this matter I referred to it as a good treaty, and I still believe it is a good treaty. It is, of course, not a perfect one, but I doubt if we had had months of discussion at San Francisco that we would have made it a better one. It restores Japanese sovereignty, but that sovereignty will be confined to the four main islands of the Japanese empire. It places no restrictions on Japan's economy or on Japan's ability to defend itself. Most important of all, the treaty sets Japan free to pursue a peaceful destiny, as we all must hope, and gives her an opportunity to contribute to the security and stability of the whole Pacific area.
The treaty was negotiated, as I explained last October, through diplomatic channels rather than through the more normal conference procedure. That was unusual procedure admittedly, but it was one which was made necessary by the circumstances. As early as 1947, the United States government had proposed to its allies a conference for the feigning of the Japanese peace treaty in the usual way. This procedure was impossible because of the attitude taken at that time

and subsequently by the Soviet union, which insisted that any such treaty should be negotiated not by a conference where all those who participated in the war against Japan would be present, but in the presence of the council of foreign ministers which would have given the U.S.S.R. and other members of the council a veto.
To avoid this procedure and the use of the veto in this connection, in September 1950 I believe it was the President of the United States initiated diplomatic discussions with the other countries represented on the Far Eastern commission with a view to negotiation by such discussion of a treaty, the final text of which we have before us today. The Canadian government participated in those discussions and was given ample opportunity to express its opinions on the various drafts as they were presented. These opinions of ours were not always accepted, Mr. Speaker, but the text which we have before us now does not represent the complete views of any one country which participated in those discussions, and is essentially a compromise document.
The Soviet union was kept fully informed of these discussions while they took place, but contributed little to them except abuse. When the conference was called in San Francisco to put the finishing touches on this process, not to negotiate a treaty but to sign one and go over the text of the draft which we have before us, the Soviet union and its satellite states were represented. As hon. members know, they refused, as indeed some other countries refused, to sign the draft.
The territorial adjustments are outlined in the treaty. The Potsdam proclamation of the treaty of peace Japan undertook to- surrender of Japan, provided that Japanese sovereignty would be limited to the four major islands and such minor islands as the allied powers would determine. Chapter II of the peace treaty carries out those surrender terms. Japan renounces all rights, title and claim to Korea, Formosa, the Pescadores, the Kurile Islands and South Sakhalin. In addition, she renounces any rights she had with respect to the islands which she held under the terms of a league of nations mandate. Under article 3 of the treaty Japan retains residual sovereignty in the Ryukyu islands and other islands to the south and southeast of Japan which were after the surrender of Japan under United States administration. Japan has agreed to concur in any proposal to place those islands under United Nations trusteeship, with the United States as the administering authority.
55704-83J
Japanese Peace Treaty
It might have been better, and it certainly would have been neater, if the final disposition of the former Japanese territories had been defined precisely in the treaty, but it was not possible for the allied powers to reach agreement on this score. It was decided, therefore, in order that the peace treaty should not be further delayed, to have Japan simply renounce her rights in these territories, as she was required to do, and to leave to future international agreement the final disposition of the territories in question-including, incidentally, Formosa.
In addition to our general Canadian interest in a peace settlement which would return Japan to normal and friendly relations with the free world, Canada had certain special concerns which were made known at every stage of the negotiations and indeed at San Francisco itself. My colleague the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), who was with me at the San Francisco conference, gave the house a full account on March 11 last of the-as we think it to be-successful agreement on North Pacific fisheries which was reached with Japan and the United States in December of last year. Under article 9 of the treaty of peace Japan undertook to- . . . enter promptly into negotiations with the Allied Powers so desiring for the conclusion of bilateral and multilateral agreements providing for the regulation or limitation of fishing and the conservation and development of fisheries on the high seas.
The promptness with which Japan entered into these negotiations is, I think, an encouraging evidence of Japan's interest in living up to the trust which has been placed in her by this treaty of peace. I think it is also a good sign for future Canadian-Japanese relations which will be entering a new chapter when this treaty is ratified.
I do not intend to go into the substance of this convention since the house has already been given the details concerning it by my colleague the Minister of Fisheries. I would remind the house, however, that until the peace treaty comes into effect Japan will not be in a position to sign the fisheries convention. We can, therefore, by ratifying the peace treaty, assist in enabling Japan to sign and ratify this important convention.
A further question in which Canada was especially interested was that of Japan's undertaking with respect to commercial practices and agreements. I made clear the views of the Canadian government on this important matter in my statement in San Francisco. Possibly it would be desirable if

Japanese Peace Treaty
I now put on the record what I then said. At the San Francisco conference I said:
Japan agrees in the treaty to conform to internationally accepted fair trade practices. It is the confident hope of my government that Japan, in the future conduct of its commercial relations with other countries, will avoid certain pre-war practices which were widely condemned at that time by other trading nations. Canada has no wish to see any discrimination against or any unnecessary obstacles to normal Japanese trade. On the contrary, as a trading nation ourselves we wish to see Japan develop its full trading possibilities. It is only common sense for us to wish for a prosperous rather than a poor Japan. Such prosperity, however, can never, in the long run, be established or even assisted by trading practices considered unfair by other countries and against which those countries have no alternative but to protect themselves if unhappily they should be adopted.
The peace treaty itself, as hon. members no doubt know, is not designed to settle questions of commercial policy but leaves this policy to be decided by the individual signatories of the treaty and Japan. Canadian attitudes and Canadian policy with respect to future commercial relations with Japan will, to a large extent, be influenced by whether or not Japan adheres to the declaration made in the preamble to the treaty of her intention, and I quote from that preamble:
... in public and private trade and commerce to conform to internationally accepted fair practices.
Another important section of the treaty deals with reparations. Critics of the treaty of peace in some countries have concentrated their attentions on the reparations clauses which represent an attempt to make this treaty an important step toward breaking the vicious cycle of "war-victory-peace-war". The allied powers recognize in the treaty that Japan should in principle pay reparations for the devastation and suffering she caused during the war. They recognize in addition, however, that Japan lacks the physical capacity to recompense her former victims if at the same time she is to achieve a viable economy and contribute to the economic health of the Pacific area. For certain nations represented at San Francisco who had not only lost property valued in billions of dollars but also countless lives, as a result of Japan's military activities, the very limited reparations clauses could not but appear unsatisfactory. For others it was easier to understand that the exaction of even just reparations might impose such an economic burden on the defeated state as to vitiate the objectives of the treaty as a whole.
In the treaty Japan undertook to compensate those allied powers whose territories she had occupied, and I quote from article 14 of the treaty:
... by making available the services of the Japanese people in production, salvaging and other work.

Negotiations are already under way at the present time on this matter between Japan and Indonesia and Japan and the Philippines. Japan further agreed in the treaty to make available certain of her assets to indemnify members of the allied forces who had suffered undue hardships while prisoners of war of Japan. This matter is covered in article 16. The details of this scheme are at the present time being worked out between the allied governments concerned and the international committee of the Red Cross which is to be responsible for the distribution of the funds in question.
Finally, the treaty provides that Japan shall return all allied property which she held during the war years upon application to be made within nine months of the coming into force of the treaty.
A highly important section of the treaty deals with security. Under article 5 of the treaty Japan undertakes to settle its international disputes by peaceful means, to refrain in its international relations from the threat or the use of force and to give the United Nations every assistance in action taken in accordance with the charter. In return, the allied powers recognize Japan's sovereign right of individual or collective self-defence.
Article 6 provides for the termination of the occupation not later than 90 days after the treaty comes into force. However, it is stated explicitly in the treaty that there is nothing in this provision to prevent the stationing or retention of foreign armed forces in Japan under the terms of any agreement made between Japan and one or more of the allied powers. The peace treaty simply recognizes for Japan the principle which article 51 of the charter of the United Nations recognizes for all sovereign states. Hence, on the very day of the signature of the peace treaty, a security treaty between the United States and Japan was signed under the terms of which Japan granted to the United States the right, upon the coming into force of the treaty of peace, to dispose United States land, air and sea forces in and about Japan. That is an exceedingly important provision. These forces are to be utilized to contribute to the maintenance of international peace and security in the Far East and indeed to the security of Japan itself against an armed attack. A United States-Japan administrative agreement implementing this security treaty was signed last month in Tokyo.
I believe the Japanese people are now aware of the tragic folly of aggressive war and that they would resist any attempt on the part of their leaders to follow the paths of conquest which they travelled in the thirties and in the early forties. In addition,

Japan is not now physically capable of following such a course; she has lost much of her former empire with all the raw materials it provided, her armed forces were completely demobilized during the occupation and her stockpiles of munitions were destroyed.
The way for the revival of aggressive militarism in Japan is not now, nor I hope will it be in the future, easy or open. It must be our hope that Japan will see the advantages to be gained from association with the free world and will co-operate in the collective defence arrangements already in being so as to contribute to the stability of that important area of the world.
Nevertheless, just as is the case with Germany in Europe, so we must at times worry about the emergence again in the Pacific of this great and powerful people, whose capacity for good can be great but whose capacity for harm, in the past, has also been great.
I have dealt only briefly with the most important provisions of the treaty, and I have not even attempted to consider some of its articles. Many of these articles provide for the necessary legal termination of the state of war which existed between Japan and the allied powers. I again commend the treaty and its attached documents to the approval of the house as a good treaty, and as an attempt to mark the end of the method of peace-making which has imposed rigid controls and galling restrictions, only to court evasion and eventual disregard.
The Japanese have, I think, in almost seven years of undisturbed occupation earned the right to have their freedom. The allied powers can at least hope by generosity to exchange a former enemy for a friend, in an area torn by strife and aggression at the present time, a friend with a proven ability which can be turned to the benefit of the Pacific area as a whole.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT SAN FRANCISCO SEPTEMBER 8, 1951
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in following the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) perhaps I shall be somewhat more expansive. However, at the beginning may I indicate to the house that the official opposition, for which at the moment I am spokesman in the debate, endorses and approves the resolution moved by the minister.
This peace treaty is perhaps the most unique of its kind in the whole of diplomatic history. It is unique, so far as its methods, procedures and negotiations are concerned. In addition to that it is unique in its constructiveness and in its lack of severe penalties inflicted upon a vanquished nation.
Japanese Peace Treaty
I was struck by the. closing observations at the San Francisco meeting by the presidential representative, who had so much to do with the negotiation of the treaty itself. I refer to Mr. John Foster Dulles. I think his words, as reported from the conference, deserve to be placed on the records of this House of Commons. He indicated that this was a question of a good peace now or a better peace never, and went on to say this:
It contains no doubt imperfections. No one is completely satisfied. But it is a good treaty. It does not contain the seeds of another war. It is truly a treaty of peace.
And at another point in his address he said this:	i
This treaty is good to the point where it cannot be made better without its becoming worse. Better words might theoretically be found; but to seek these is to let escape what is now within our grasp. There come times when to seek the perfect is to lose the good. This is such a time.
It was our common hope that out of the fiery purge of war there would rise a new Japan. That was no foolish hope. Japan has a great culture and tradition which are capable of producing distinctively. but no less authentically, those virtues which all nations and peoples must possess if there is to be a world-wide commonwealth of peace.
In order, however, that that potentiality shall become actuality, Japan needs free political institutions in a climate conducive to their vigorous growth; social progress; an equal administration of justice; an awareness of human dignity; a sense of self-respect, of respect for others. Above all Japan needs the will to live at peace with others as good neighbours.
All this is possible, if we make peace now. It becomes impossible, or at best improbable, if Japan's long deferred hopes are now blasted.
There are, in Japan, new-born institutions of freedom. They will not flourish if military rule continues indefinitely to be supreme.
The United States, which since the surrender has directed occupation on behalf of all the allies, says solemnly to each of the allies: unless you now give Japan peace and freedom on such honourable terms as have been negotiated, the situation will rapidly deteriorate.
It is time to end the subjection of the Japanese government to allied command. It is time to end the occupation and to recognize that, henceforth, it is the Japanese people who exercise complete sovereignty in Japan. It is time to welcome Japan as an equal and honourable member of the family of nations. That is what the pending treaty will do.
It is on that general basis that this parliament may be expected to support the resolution now moved by the minister. When I am developing that point I should like to pay tribute to the work done by the presidential representative on that occasion, Mr. John Foster Dulles. It was a painstaking, it was a tedious, and I have no doubt at times it was a disappointing task. But his perseverance, his resolution and his determination to see that there was a peace treaty for Japan never ended, with the result that one of the newspapers in another country said that his success in connection with the Japanese peace

Japanese Peace Treaty
treaty was a feather in the somewhat battered cap of American diplomacy and American leadership during these years.
That is not necessarily in all its terms a reflection of my thought with respect to American diplomacy and leadership. But I wish to indicate at least that Mr. Dulles' position is, I believe, appreciated by the free world on this occasion..
I wish if I may to mention another personality, and I hope that in doing so I shad not be accused of entering into the general election campaign in the United States. Our own campaigns are difficult enough without taking on the task in another land. But I do want to mention General MacArthur. Whatever one may think of his military or political judgment in fields other than the occupation of Japan, I think we must admit, and freely admit, that General MacArthur did a statesmanlike job with respect to his occupation duties in Japan from the end of the war until he was released from his duties. One of the most orderly and normal transitions from war to peace occurred during that period. It was I think an indication of where we could properly apply and did apply reason instead of revenge in our dealings with those who were the losers in- a world war.
I think some of the things which he instituted have had a great deal to do perhaps with the present success of our friendly relations with Japan so far as the free powers of the world go. I need only to mention one or two in order to indicate what was done. There was the destruction of the power of the war lords and those politicians in Japan who had been responsible for the war itself; there was the breaking up of the family cartel system; a measure of land reform was introduced; female suffrage was granted for the first time; and in addition there was the breaking up of the insidious relationship between the government and shintoism. It was a sound bit of statesmanship and I think whatever may be said about General MacArthur in other fields he deserves credit for the kind of leadership that he gave in a very difficult and critical time in the relations of other free nations with the nation known as Japan.
I want to make reference if I may to what I think is our outmoded system of dealing with treaties such as this. I think our system borders on being a relic of yesterday. I do not think we should be handling a treaty like this one in the way we are, to have it appear simply as a government notice of motion on the order paper without the opportunity to discuss it fully even in committee of the whole house and the minister being able to answer questions only when he finishes the debate. I do not think that is
IMr. Graydon.]
good enough so far as our parliamentary procedure is concerned.
I am not critical in any way of the minister because after all he is simply following the dictates of our parliamentary procedure. We have in this treaty twenty-one pages of fairly closely written clauses, dozens of documents are cited and there are nine complicated protocols and conventions in the declaration alone which none of us have so far seen. In addition to that, several departments of government are involved.
When we have no machinery for dealing with it in committee of the whole I would be quite satisfied to have it dealt with in the standing committee on external affairs. I am supported in that by the fact that in our own Senate they have endorsed the principle of the resolution, as I am endorsing the principle this evening, and when they return somewhere around the end of April or the first of May they will proceed to deal with the treaty clause by clause in their foreign relations committee.
I notice that in Great Britain they deal with these things differently from what we do. I am not so sure that we should not follow Great Britain in dealing with treaties of this kind. There the treaty is brought forward in the form of a bill which is given first reading, second reading, considered in committee and then given third reading. It then goes on to the House of Lords. I read with a good deal of interest what was said on this treaty both on the second reading stage and during the committee stage. It received careful examination and I felt that those who took part in the debate had an exceptional knowledge of the situation as it existed.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF TREATY SIGNED AT SAN FRANCISCO SEPTEMBER 8, 1951
speechtext:
I am glad to have the minister's explanation on that. My point is that this resolution ought to go to the external affairs committee. It seems to me that before we endorse a treaty of this kind the fullest information ought to be available to the members and to the house. I do not think there is any desire on the part of anyone to place any obstacles in the way of the passage of this commendable treaty, but I do urge that this matter be sent to the external affairs committee before the bill is introduced.
I was interested in reading the debates which took place in the foreign relations committee of the Senate of the United States and also in the Senate itself. Perhaps this is a most appropriate time to mention this

as we have just had a budget speech and there are signs of fatigue on every side of the house. When the Senate of the United States dealt with the Japanese treaty it was found that they did not have a quorum of senators. I think that indicates that so far as our national boundaries are concerned there is not such a great difference. The minister has hinted at some urgency in connection with this matter. I would point out that the sixth nation out of the eleven which is necessary to give a majority to provide for the implementation of the treaty was Pakistan. I understand that just a couple of days ago Pakistan approved and ratified the treaty with Japan. I should be glad to go further in my argument to have this referred to the standing committee on external affairs, but perhaps that will not be necessary.
As I see it, there are many questions in the public mind in connection with this treaty that will have to be answered. There is the question of trade, the question of commercial practices, the question of fishery rights, the question of reparations, the question of maritime enterprise, the question of immigration and other questions affecting the social and economic as well as the diplomatic side of the treaty. Some of these matters are extremely delicate in their complexion and design. I am going to leave that suggestion with the minister as it stands in the hope he will accept it. I think he will find there is no delay of a dangerous character involved because the Senate does not come back until the first of May anyway and they will only start to deal with the question at that time.
Following the minister's remarks with respect to the treaty itself in which he said that it did mark the formal conclusion of the state of war, it is also, if I may say so, a step in the right direction of rebuilding the stability and security of the Pacific area. If there is any area at the moment outside of Europe itself that needs attention with respect to rebuilding and security it is that very area. It was pointed out in the British house by Kenneth Younger, M.P., formerly minister of state in the Attlee government, that Japan was in the very nest of problems because there was great communist China on one side, Soviet Russia on the other, and Japan herself, all three at the one time major powers. In addition to that there is the legitimate interest of Britain and the United States and other powers in that very locality. Japan is in a sense sitting on almost the powder keg of the world. I have no doubt that is one of the reasons why this treaty is so unique in its provisions so far as leniency to the Japanese government and Japanese people is concerned.
Japanese Peace Treaty
1 think one of the things one gathers from a reading of the treaty is that in a sense it serves as a base from which to approach the wider area of issues because we must not make the mistake of thinking that the treaty by any means settles all the issues either surrounding Japan or in Japan itself. It only takes a step towards solution of them, and Japan's relations with the free world on many fronts remain unsettled and undefined. But it does point the way to such settlement, and half a loaf of course is sometimes better than none. Giving Japan her sovereignty and admitting her into what we think is respectable international society has involved risks. Those risks of course belong to the military, economic and other fields, but on the other hand we had to take some calculated risks in connection with this matter.
One of the things that struck me most was the attitude of the Australian government. The Australian government has interests in that area that perhaps we do not have in quite the same measure. I do not mean to convey that our interests are not of a very important character too but Australia came within an ace of being occupied by the Japanese forces. In reviewing the Japanese treaty the prime minister of Australia, Mr. Menzies, says something which I think is significant. He has this to say:
... it is simple to understand that the instinctive reaction of Australia to any proposal for a Japanese peace settlement is, "Keep them down! Don't let them rearm! Don't trust them!" It is true that history proves that such reactions are ephemeral and sometimes dangerous. But we are not living in a world of historians; we are living in a world of men and women, of widowed wives and bereaved mothers; a world tenaciously attached to a justice which precedes mercy, though it may be tempered by it . . . The United States and the United Kingdom, the two principal free nations, made it clear that they were not prepared to prohibit a substantial measure of Japanese rearmament. And if these great powers were not willing to prohibit, and to enforce that prohibition by supervision and occupation if necessary, how could Australia by herself make a prohibition effective? To that question there was, and is, no real answer.
Then he goes on to say:
Japan is destined once more, and very rapidly to be a great industrial power. To prohibit this successfully would be to condemn the most virile people in East Asia to poverty, misery and revolution. No greater threat to Asiatic peace could be imagined. To prohibit it unsuccessfully would be to make the worst of both worlds, for power and hatred would be renewed together. Japan will again become a great industrial power more rapidly than she can become a military power; in her case the one depends so much upon the other. But during the intervening period an undefended Japan would be a constant temptation and an easy prey for the territorial imperialism of the communists. We must not forget that one of the checks upon aggression today is the fact that, with western Germany and Japan outside the Soviet orbit, the balance of heavy industrial production weighs down heavily in favour of the free world. Japan must therefore be defended. By whom? Putting aside the question of how far and

Japanese Peace Treaty
how long any democracy will be prepared to maintain an army of occupation in a defeated country, a question full of not only economic but psychological and moral considerations, let me look once more at the pure sentiment of it. Armies of occupation in Japan must, having regard to the communist threat, have two functions. One is to keep the peace in Japan against the Japanese. So far our feelings are satisfied. But the other function must be to defend Japan against an external attacker. It would come as a shock to most Australians to be told that as a punishment for the Japanese, Australian troops were in future to defend Japan while the Japanese themselves went smiling and bowing about their affairs of production and commerce. . . The case for a measure of Japanese rearmament is thus complete unless the great powers, that is, the United States and the United Kingdom, are able and willing to do on the grand scale what I am sure Australia would not want to do for any length of time on the small scale.
Then he goes on further to say:
. . . we should be foolish to force a hard and bitter peace upon Japan because we feared that in fifteen or twenty years' time Japan might once more become an aggressor, when the real and deadly and present question is whether, inside the next two years, we shall between us be strong enough to resist, and therefore deter, a vast communist aggression against one manifestation of which we are actually now fighting in Korea. If the United States, with its tremendous world responsibility and its magnificent and unprecedented preparation to discharge it, chooses to see Japan not as a possible future danger but as a present and important factor in world defensive strategy against communism, who can with confidence gamble upon the future course of history and say that it is wrong? And in any case, the United States is taking its risk prudently. Pursuant to article 6 of the treaty the United States is entering into a defensive pact with Japan. Thus, by a double stroke, Japan is made a co-operator in the short-range defence problem and a potential friend in the long run. There are, of course, many people who feel that the Japanese people have, by the joint effects of defeat and occupation, "suffered a sea change" into democracy. I do not believe this for a moment. Democracy is a growth from the soil; it is never imposed from without. Witness the easy and swift collapse of parliamentary selfgovernment in Germany and Italy. It needs a tree with deep roots in a deep soil to withstand the winter gales of tyranny. The real question is not whether Japan has already become democratic (a notion which I frankly do not believe), but whether, to quote the recent words of my colleague, Mr. R. G. Casey, "to permit the Japanese people to recover their self-respect and some measure of economic independence offers the best means of promoting the growth of a workable democracy in Japan."
Then Mr. Menzies goes on:
It is my own deep belief that, though slavery is the breeding ground of revolution, only freedom and free men can bring forth democracy.
Coming from the head of the state which perhaps has more reason to be nervous because of the resurgence of Japan as a great power than almost any other country in the free world, I think that at least gives some indication how far nations are prepared to go in endorsing this plan for dealing with Japan.

I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the question to be asked concerning this treaty, which is sometimes described as the softest in the diplomatic history of the world, is simple; and we are giving it a simple answer. The question is, do we want and do we need 83 million Japanese people with us in our efforts to keep the world free and at peace? The answer we are giving is shown by our approval of the resolution now before the house. That answer is yes, as far as the people of Canada are concerned. This treaty will give Japan a chance, by entering into an alliance with the free nations of the world, to link her power in the Orient with that of the United Kingdom, the United States and other countries. I am satisfied, as I am sure the Japanese people are satisfied, that her future is better with us than it would be if she were absorbed into the net of Russian imperialism. If Japan behaves herself in the free world society she has an opportunity to again become a great leader in the Orient. With the soviet it would be a different proposition. Many reasons could be advanced as to why Japan would throw in her lot with us rather than with the soviet regime, to be interlocked and interwoven with that extensive international mechanism known as imperial communism. There she would lose not only her identity and her opportunity to become a great power again; she would also lose her internal relationship with her emperor, which to the Japanese people is still a very important consideration.
As the minister indicated a few moments ago, many of the United States forces will be remaining in Japan, not as occupation forces but under the terms of the security treaty which has been entered into between the United States and Japan. I,think this has a bearing on one of the things some of us on this side of the house have been arguing for, without very much effect as yet though I am hoping the day will come when we will be able to tell the minister we are glad he has accepted our suggestion. I refer to the question of a Pacific pact. I am sure the minister must be thinking, "I have answered that fellow so often, surely he must be convinced by now that we cannot do anything about it at this stage." Nevertheless I mention the matter again because I think we have a further argument now by virtue of entering into the Japanese treaty. We cannot go on forever in the Pacific having all these pacts and alliances, without having some kind of master pact to combine them all. We now have a pact between the United States and Australia and New Zealand. We have a pact between United States and Japan, and we have a pact between the United States and the Philippines. These all being mutual

security pacts, it seems to me the time is coming when we must have an over-all plan. I think I may interpret the words of Mr. Dean Acheson, Secretary of State for the United States, in that way when he appeared before the senate foreign relations committee during the debate two months ago. This was the only statement made by Mr. Acheson, I think, which has any relation to the problem I am discussing. This is what he said:
The ratification of these treaties would give courage and hope to millions of people in the Pacific area, whose primary desire is to live at peace with their neighbours. It is our hope that these treaties will serve as a point of departure for the development of an effective system of regional security in the Pacific.
You will note the words "serve as a point of departure"; and with that I rest my case again. I am sure if the minister moves from his present rather static position with respect to the Pacific pact, he will find himself once more in the company of a man in whose company he finds himself perhaps more often than any other diplomat in the world. I am hoping he will follow some of these men who are more experienced than the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) who during a debate in this house some weeks ago chided the party I represent for advocating such expensive things as the Pacific pact. That was the first time anyone on the government side said it was money that was behind our delay, our reluctance, our refusal to join a Pacific pact. So I hope the minister will take to heart what has been said by a man whom I consider to be rather more experienced in foreign affairs than the hon. member for Coast-Capilano.
A glance at the map of this area will show the great problems which arise from a geographical point of view. There are four islands, Hokkaido to the north, Honshu to the south, Shikoku and Kyushu. I hope I am pronouncing them properly. The minister has not corrected me, so perhaps he does not know any more about it than I do. It is interesting to note that between the northern island of Hokkaido and Russian occupied island of Sakhalin there is a strait only some 60 or 75 miles wide. There is only 200 miles between Honshu and Korea, which indicates that Japan is in the very centre of trouble. She is a close neighbour of red China and also a close neighbour of soviet Russia, and all the time needing raw materials and markets. Those of us who have watched the progress of the Moscow trade conference during the last day or so will recognize, of course, that on the trade front the soviet are again attempting to make a dent in our flank. No doubt they are not overlooking in that meeting the problems which face Japan economically. Not only are they attempting to call a bluff on Japan so far as trade is
Japanese Peace Treaty concerned, but also to sabotage by a movement through the northern island of Hokkaido, which has its origin in Sakhalin to the north. In addition to that, at the moment Japan faces a need for food, for iron, for coking coal and for raw materials for the textile industry. As one member in the British house said, Japan is the only oriental country that has actually measured up to the western world in so far as both technology and production are concerned.
In the past one of Japan's problems has been to try to find the raw materials for 83 million people who are engaged in such extensive and intensive production. This problem got her into trouble before. During the depression Japan's trade practices were largely criticized from one end of the world to the other. She found herself in a very tight corner with respect to these markets and raw materials. One of the problems we shall have to face I think is this. If Japan gets into a tight corner economically, the soviets will take advantage of the situation at every turn. Already the soviets have offered coal to Japan for a third of the price at which it can be delivered from the United States. I believe that is an indication of what Japan, and incidentally this country, have before us by way of problems in the Far East.
In addition to that, of course, the pressure to recognize and deal with red China is great. Some time ago Premier Yoshida of Japan indicated his close attraction for the government on Formosa in contrast to that of red China. Nevertheless, it was not long ago, perhaps a year ago, that the same premier made a statement which I think is evidence of the danger that faces us in that area. He said:
Red or white, China remains our next door neighbour-economical law will, I believe, prevail in the long run over ideological differences.
I had intended going somewhat further afield in connection with my argument concerning the treaty, but the time is getting late. I am going to close by leaving out the matter of Japan's problem with communism in that area. It is an interesting story, but it is a story that perhaps can be told on another occasion. One of the things we ought to consider very carefully is that Japan is going to need help, and she is going to need understanding from the other sections of the free world in order to restore her position and to permanently retain it. Whatever we may do by way of this treaty of peace, it still remains an uneasy peace for Japan. It is our obligation, it is our duty to do our best to make that peace as firm a peace for the Japanese people as we can.
The admission of Japan into free world circles poses hard-cored problems for Canada.

Japanese Peace Treaty
The minister mentioned two of them. Apparently the problem of fisheries has been reasonably well solved, according to the minister, but naturally one would like to examine more closely what that convention actually includes. I intended to put on the record tonight the story of the imports and exports so far as Japan and Canada were concerned both in 1938-39 and since the war. I believe it would show that the balance generally has been in our favour, which indicates I think that in most instances trade with Japan on a normal, proper and fair basis cannot do this country any harm and will do the Japanese economy a great deal of good. I believe our job will be to find a solution to the problem of preventing Japan from being thrown, economically and commercially, into the hands of communists. At the same time we must maintain our position with respect to trade so that our standard of living and the working people of Canada are protected. I am satisfied a solution of that problem can be arrived at without attempting in any way to throttle the economy of Japan. I believe that we can get together and, without harm to our own industries here, find a large field of trade upon which to draw in order to keep Japan free, even in that disturbed area.
One of the main problems is, of course, in connection with the arbitrary clause in our Customs Act respecting dumping. If Japan becomes a member of the Geneva agreement on trade and tariffs, that section may be put in jeopardy again. I am satisfied these are matters that can be solved, and I am not raising them except to indicate the serious problems that are ahead of us. For many long years the United Kingdom and Japan were faithful allies. Prior to the early twenties their friendship and ours was almost traditional. Today we are witnessing the restoration of that international bond of mutual understanding between the free world and Japan. All I can say, Mr. Speaker, is: May it usher in a new and more constructively peaceful era in our Pacific relations.
On motion of Mr. Coldwell the debate was adjourned.

The first part of 1951 was dominated by strong inflationary pressures, but as the year progressed these became somewhat less severe. The underlying inflationary potential is still high but for the time being, at least, it appears to be under control.
A brief review of the post-war years will put our present problems in perspective. The years 1946 to 1948 were a period of transition from war to peace. This transition was achieved more smoothly and with rather less disturbance than many Canadians had feared. In Canada, as in other countries, we experienced in this period a greater rise in prices than had been expected, but the redeployment of labour from the armed services and the war industries to the tasks of peace was accomplished with far less unemployment and industrial dislocation than most people had dared to hope.
By mid-1948 the reconversion of industry and the redeployment of labour had been largely completed, and for nearly two years, from the summer of 1948 to the late spring of 1950 Canada enjoyed a period of relative economic equilibrium at high levels of employment and income. Price levels remained stable and employment remained high, and not even the sharp United States recession of 1949 nor the devaluation crisis in September of that year seriously disturbed the balance of the Canadian economy.
The spring of 1950 saw the beginning of what seemed to be a new sustained upswing in Canadian economic activity, sparked by a rapid acceleration in the discovery and development of natural resources and re-enforced by the quick rebound in the United States from its recession of the previous summer. Even before the outbreak of hostilities in Korea, 1950 showed signs of developing a situation in which our resources would be fully extended in meeting the programmes of peaceful economic expansion which the Canadian people had set for themselves.
The Korean aggression, with the grave threats it exposed and the serious alarms it engendered, initiated a scramble for inventories all over the world. The world market prices of many staple raw materials-wool, tin, rubber, copper, lead, zinc, oils and fats, hides, cotton and chemicals-rose sharply, and within six months had gone up as much as 50, 100 and even 200 per cent.
The first phase of this new inflationary cycle was largely psychological, stemming as it did from a fear of shortages and higher prices and a consequent scramble for inventories and replacements. Consumers participated in this scramble, particularly in the field of cars and household equipment and appliances. But the real inflationary force created by Korea flowed fundamentally from the necessity and determination throughout the Western world to carry through a speedy and a heavy defensive rearmament programme. The magnitude of the defence programme adopted was clearly one that could not be inserted into an already fully extended economy. To accomplish this defence programme in the time allotted it was necessary simultaneously to restrain consumption, encourage savings, increase productive efficiency and capacity, forego less essential forms of capital expansion, and divert labour and materials to defence and to defence supporting industries.
In a free democratic country governments do not dictate the course of economic affairs, but governments can and should follow policies which guide or steer the economy in the right direction. The general import of government policies should contribute toward restraint where restraint is needed and toward expansion where expansion is needed.

The Budget-Appendix
Federal financial and economic policies have been designed to these ends. Consumer spending has been restrained by means of higher personal taxes and higher commodity taxes, especially on commodities that make heavy demands upon critical materials or other critical resources. Monetary policy has been such as to discourage the expansion of credit generally and consumer spending has also been restrained by the Consumer Credit Regulations. Greater savings have been encouraged directly through the more attractive terms of the sixth series of Canada Savings Bonds, as well as by the restraints on spending and by the increase in interest rates generally which has resulted from the rising demand for loan funds in the face of a limited supply.
Capital expansion in the form of new plant and equipment has been restricted in the case of projects which are less essential in the context of present conditions and encouraged in the case of projects related to the broad needs of defence. This selective approach has been made both through the priorities and allocations policies administered by the Department of Defence Production and through the operations of the "deferred depreciation" regulations administered by the Department of Trade and Commerce. In a limited number of cases essential expansion in defence industries has been facilitated by the granting of accelerated depreciation on specialized new plant and equipment, or by direct capital assistance with government funds.
The greater difficulty of borrowing and the higher level of interest rates generally have had a moderating influence on investment in new capital projects, particularly marginal projects, and on investment in inventories.

The general economic position in the opening months of 1952 is that the inflationary pressures have been brought under control, but that at many points in the economy a strong inflationary potential still exists. Any series of adverse events which sharply raised the present international tensions could bring about a renewal of direct inflationary pressures that might seriously test our economic defences. But at the moment the prospects for 1952 indicate continued high levels of employment and general business activity, without any renewal of overt inflation, and with most of the increased output occurring in the defence and defence supporting sections of the economy.
The inflationary pressures that persist are not evenly distributed through the economy. At some points and in some regions the economy is likely to be fully or more than fully extended. At other points and in other regions the available resources are likely to fall short of full utilization. While these contrasting situations will not persist indefinitely, it may take time to adjust them since resources both in labour and in plant and equipment are not fully or easily transferable, either technically or geographically.

THE NATIONAL ACCOUNTS National Income, Product and Expenditure
National Income is the total of the annual earnings of Canadian residents from the production of goods and services. As such it includes salaries, wages and other forms of employee earnings in cash or in kind, as well as military pay and allowances. It includes corporation profits, interest, net rent, and the net income of farmers and others who are in business on their own account.
Gross National Product is the value at market prices of all the goods and services produced in a year by the labour, capital, and enterprise of Canadian residents. It is measured by adding together the costs of production. Part of these costs of production are the factor costs or, more simply, the earnings of the factors of production, labour, capital and enterprise; and the total of these factor costs is National Income. Indirect taxes and other costs such as depreciation allowances also enter into the cost of goods and services although they do not form part of the income of Canadians. They are, therefore, added to National Income to obtain Gross National Product. Subsidies on the other hand may be regarded as offsets to costs of production and are therefore deducted.
Gross National Expenditure measures the same aggregate as Gross National Product but in a different way. The goods and services produced in a year are either sold at home or abroad or added to inventories. Thus Gross National Expenditure is obtained by adding together all sales and adjusting them for imports and changes in inventories. While Canadian expenditure on imported goods and services is included in the total sales to consumers, to governments, and to business for capital account, it is not part of the disposition of Canadian production and is therefore deducted. But since foreign expenditures on Canadian goods and services, i.e., exports, form part of the earnings of Canadians in the Gross National Product, they are included in Gross National Expenditure.

National Income and Product
Gross National Product reached $21,241 million in 1951, an increase of 17 per cent over 1950. After allowing for the upward movement of prices which amounted to 11 per cent, it is estimated that the real increase in product was rather more than 5 per cent.
Since the present estimates of change in real product are only approximate, they must be used with some caution in assessing the importance of the gain for a given year or in comparing it with other years. However, it appears that the percentage gain in real product for 1951 was greater than the increase during 1950 and comparable to the combined increases of the two years 1948 and
1949.	A significant factor in the increase in product, and one which did not operate in 1950 was the growth in the employed labour force of about 2\ per cent. This was partly offset, however, by a decline of 1 per cent in average weekly hours worked.
A substantial part of the estimated 5 per cent increase in real product, perhaps one-quarter, was due to increased agricultural production, particularly the western grain crop. Because of poor weather, part of this crop remained unharvested in 1951 and thus constituted an involuntary addition to inventories. It is an increase in real product which remains to some extent in doubt, and one which had no positive impact on the economy in 1951. Elsewhere in the economy, although output was higher for the year as a whole, some significant changes occurred during the course of the year in both the pace and pattern of production. Thus while the index of industrial production averaged 212-0 for 1951, or 6-9 per cent above the average for 1950, it rose to a peak of 223-4 in May from which it declined to 200-3 in December. A very significant factor in this rise and decline was the change in demand for consumer goods, particularly durables and textiles which weakened greatly after the first four months of the year, and resulted in a sharp curtailment of production. The increase in expenditures for defence and resource development, which became more important as the year advanced, was not sufficient to offset the effects of reduced demand for consumer goods, so that the index fell at year end below the levels reached late

In addition to the estimated increase of more than 5 per cent in Canadian real product, imports of goods and services exceeded exports by $534 million in 1951 compared with an excess of $329 million in 1950. This increased product went for defence and capital purposes, many of which were defence supporting, rather than for consumer expenditure. Personal Income and Its Disposition
For the purpose of showing the relationship between the incomes, spending and saving of Canadians, Personal Income is a more useful concept than National Income.
Personal Income differs from National Income in a number of ways. It is defined as the sum of current receipts of income regardless of whether these receipts are earnings from production. Thus it includes only that part of corporation profits which is actually received by Canadian persons as dividends. Similarly deductions must also be made from employees' total earnings for unemployment insurance contributions or pension contributions which, although forming part of the compensation for services performed, are not actually received by the employee within the year. On the other hand, transfer payments such as family allowances, old age pensions, veterans' benefits and charitable contributions of corporations, are part of personal income although they are not payments for services and, therefore, do not form part of National Income.

A special adjustment is necessary for farm income since the farmer does not receive full payment for his grain at the time it is delivered to the Wheat Board. An initial payment is made upon delivery and subsequent payments adjust for the full price realized by the Board. Thus for a time a part of the farmer's income accumulates with the Wheat Board. Personal Income rose by $2,361 million or 18 per cent during 1951. The largest part of this increase was due to the gain of $1,312 million in salaries and wages net of employer and employee contributions to social insurance and government pension funds. Net income received by farmers rose very sharply by 52 per cent, while net incomes from other unincorporated business increased by only 5 per cent. The rise in farm receipts was accentuated by larger Wheat Board disbursements. Dividends paid out by corporations increased by 2 ner cent. Transfer payments were the only source of personal income which fell below 1950 levels and the decline in these was slight. The gain in personal income on a per capita basis appears to have been greater than the rise in prices of consumer goods and services.

Source and Disposition of Saving
Saving may be regarded as the source from which investment expenditure is financed. Income arising out of production may either be spent or saved. At the same time production will be absorbed either by consumption expenditure, or by investment expenditure at home for new plant, equipment, housing, or additions to inventory, or by investment abroad. Saving must therefore equal investment. It is, therefore, possible to construct tables which show, on the one hand, the sources of saving and, on the other, the use of these savings to finance gross investment at home or investment abroad.

The Budget-Appendix
In addition to personal saving which was mentioned there can be government saving and business saving. If, for example, governments have a surplus of revenue over expenditure, this surplus constitutes part of the nation's saving. If there are government deficits they are an offset to the total of private saving by individuals and businesses.
During 1951 the composition of saving changed substantially. Personal saving increased by $880 million, government saving by $371 million while business saying, including undistributed Wheat Board trading profits, declined by $37 million. As a result business saving in 1951 was relatively less important as a source of funds for the rapidly growing investment demand at home. Less than 45 per cent of gross domestic investment was financed from business saving during 1951, compared with almost 60 per cent in 1950.

Revenue and Expenditure of All Governments
In Table 10 "Government Transactions Related to the National Accounts" an attempt is made to bring together in one statement and under uniform headings, the activities of all governments in Canada on a calendar year basis.
The table is designed to include only those transactions which have relevance for the National Accounts, and consequently the surpluses or deficits shown here do not agree with those shown in the various public accounts. It has been necessary to adjust the conventional accounting statements of fiscal year revenue and expenditure to exclude purely bookkeeping transactions such as those relating to reserves, write-offs, amortization, and other non-cash items, as well as the purchase and sale of existing capital assets; and to include the transactions of extra-budgetary funds such as unemployment insurance, workmen's compensation and government pension funds. Government loans and investments, and debt retirement, are not included in government expenditure.
In the federal accounts, some of the more substantial adjustments are as follows: elimination of reserve for possible losses on active assets, elimination of reserve for veterans' conditional benefits, elimination of expenditures charged with respect to the assumption of Newfoundland debt in 1949, elimination of expenditures charged with respect to shipment of World War II military equipment to N.A.T.O. countries, addition of expenditures out of Defence Equipment Replacement Account, elimination of write-down of active assets to non-active account, adjustment of corporation taxes to an accrual basis, inclusion of the change in inventories of government commodity agencies and the Defence Production Revolving Fund, and elimination of sales of war assets. In addition, the federal figures are adjusted to a calendar year basis by using the monthly figures published by the Comptroller of the Treasury.
Municipalities are for the most part on a calendar year basis but the provincial figures are based on the provincial fiscal years. Because of the lack of current information the 1951 figures for provincial and municipal governments involve a considerable element of estimation.

Federal government expenditure on goods and services increased by $710 million or 73 per cent in 1951. More than 90 per cent of this increase was due to accelerated defence spending. Although the increase in defence spending was not as great as had been planned, it absorbed about one-half of the nation's increased product for 1951. This increase does not reflect the full impact of the defence program on the economy since the larger part of the increase in private capital investment during 1951 was also directed to defence and defence supporting industries. Federal non-defence spending on goods and services, on the other hand, increased by less than 10 per cent and when account is taken of price increases, the use of the nation's product for these purposes was approximately unchanged. The increase in provincial and municipal expenditure on goods and services for 1951 is estimated at 6 per cent. Here too no increase in real terms is indicated when account is taken of prices.
The combined total of transfer payments for all levels of government remained approximately unchanged from the calendar year 1950, with decreases at the federal level more or less offset by increases in provincial and municipal transfers. The major declines were in payments to veterans and in unemployment insurance benefits while increases occurred in family allowances, old age pensions and provincial and municipal grants to hospitals.

Total federal revenues for the calendar year 1951 were $1,094 million or 36 per cent higher than in 1950.
